speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1.	To Thunder Bay and Rainy River, none; to West Algoma, three; to East Algoma, eight; to Nipissing, none.
2 and 3. It was stated in the Toronto Conservative newspapers of I9th October, 1908, Mr. GRAHAM.
that a number of men, not regular constables, were being given special authority by the government of Ontario to make arrests and were to go into the constituencies of East and West Algoma in connection with the elections then proceeding, to polling places called backwoods polls to patrol the approaches to such polls on the voting day and make arrests as they might think fit. It is the ancient and undoubted privilege and right of this House to conduct its own elections by its own officials, who are responsible to it alone. The House of Commons has at all times been jealous to guard this privilege and right, and quick to resent any interference with it. In these circumstances, believing the statements in the newspapers above referred to, to be true, I, upon my own responsibility as a servant of this House, directed that sufficient Dominion police to protect honest voters from intimidation or interference with the free exercise of their franchise and under instructions to arrest and prosecute under section 269 of the Dominion Elections Act any one guilty of such indictable offences should be sent at once from Ottawa to the Electoral Districts of East and West Algoma. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
1.	From the information at present available an estimate cannot be given of the number of acres of coal lands there are in the province of Alberta. Coal has been discovered in many parts of the province, but in the large majority of cases the development of these several discoveries has not been sufficient upon which to base an estimate as to the extent of the coal-measures. In addition to this, more than one-half of the province lies north of Edmonton, and as no great demand for coal in this northern part of the province has yet arisen, very little prospecting has been carried on. New discoveries of coal in the southern portion of the province are still being made, and while it is known that the coal-measures of the province are of very great extent no estimate has been attempted as to the number of acres of such lands or the total tonnage of coal within such areas.

5.	If so, does the government consider it proper to exercise such discrimination in establishing regulations to govern administration principles, as operates to the financial gain of the permanent soldier and the financial loss of the active militia?

1. A minimum period of duration of wear is fixed for all articles of clothing issued to non-permanent units. If, after this period has expired, an article is considered by the inspecting officer fit for further service, such article must be continued in use until worn out.
2 and 3. Clothing issued to permanent units is divided into two classes, ' public property' and 'personal property.' All articles of public clothing have a fixed period of duration of wear, during which

time the militiaman is financially responsible for the same. They are continued in use beyond this period until condemned as unfit by a board of officers. Articles of personal clothing are issued at stated intervals as part of the original contract with the militiaman. If an article of personal clothing is in sufficiently good condition to last another period, compensation in lieu of issue is authorized.
4 and 5. No. This should not be the case, as articles of clothing with a fixed period of duration of say three years, are, generally speaking, only used for three annual camps, that is for thirty-six days. The only charges made against officers commanding non-permanent units are for deficiencies or damages due to carelessness or neglect.

Is the government aware that the allowance made tb the officers of the active militia to cover lodging and subsistence while attending provisional schools of instruction is fixed at one dollar per diem, while that for officers of the permenent force detailed for duty at the same schools, is fixed at two dollars and fifty cents per diem? If so, what is the basis for the discrimination in favour of the permanent force and against the active militia for the same service?

The permanent force officer makes soldiering his profession; is ordered to the provisional school, and has to be allowed a suitable rate of subsistence while away from his station.
As regards the active militia officer, the provisional school is opened in his neighbourhood at his request and to suit his convenience. Usually no allowance is paid, but, where such is granted, the same rate is paid as at the royal schools, viz., $1 per diem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TARIFF COMMISSION AT MIDDLETON, NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
A committee of ministers of the Crown, commonly spoken of as the Tariff Commission, conducted inquiries into the operation of the tariff at many places throughout the Dominion in the autumn of 1905 and the beginning of 1906. The committee sat at Middleton, Nova Scotia, on January 16, 1906, and the ministers present were the Ministers of Finance, Customs and Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur).
All the proceedings of the committee at every point were open to the public and were widely reported in the newspapers of the day. The names of all witnesses and the full report of their evidence were submitted to this House in the session of 1906 and are on file for the information of any member who may wish to consult the reports. The House of Commons ordered that these reports be not printed. The ministers made no formal report, but the information received by them, during the inquiry, was used in the revision of the tariff at the session of 1907.

That in the opinion of this House it is advisable that a commission of inquiry be forthwith appointed to investigate the needs of Canada in respect to technical education, and to report on ways and means by which these needs may be best met.
He said: During the session of this House in 1907, I had the honour to move a motion framed in terms very similar to those of the motion which I have now the honour of bringing to the attention of the House. But on that occasion the motion came up for discussion at a very late hour of the evening, and before a very thin attendance of members; the discussion was exceedingly limited, and the subject did not, I think, receive the attention which its importance deserved. I do not think that upon that occasion I was able to impress either the House or the government with the soundness of my argument, or with the propriety or necessity for the motion, strongly as I was able to impress myself. I may say that the views which I then expressed I still hold; and in presenting my case on this occasion, I shall discuss it from the same point of view as I did on the former occasion.
I hope that on the present occasion the discussion may become more general, as I am fully aware that there are many hon. members in this House far better able to discuss it than I am, men who have greater experience, more information, fuller knowledge in regard to the subject of technical education than I have. I bring it forward on this occasion, as I did on the former occasion, at the request of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, two very prominent and important bodies in this community. Both those bodies have passed very strong resolutions upon the subject, and have honoured me with the request that I bring the matter once more to the attention of this House.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association has not only taken action in concrete form upon the subject itself, but has gone to the trouble of consulting many of the men who are at the head of the leading educational institutions in this country, for the purpose Mr. BRODEUR.
of obtaining their views upon the proposal contained in this motion. I think almost without exception the association has received replies from those men who are leaders of education in this country, commending the course proposed in this motion. The association has also sought to find the opinion of the leading Boards of Trade and Chambers of Commerce in Canada on this question, and has consulted probably all the Boards of Trade and Chambers of Commerce from east to west, in all towns and cities of any consequence. Out of fifty or sixty communications received from these bodies, I think, without exception, they have passed resolutions in favour of the proposal contained in the resolution. Furthermore, the Manufacturers' Association, realizing perhaps what was the most serious objection to the proposal, have taken the trouble of consulting the premiers of the various provinces of Canada as to the necessity and propriety of the motion and as to the question of its being brought up in this parliament, and I believe that without a single exception the premiers throughout the various self-governing provinces in Canada have replied consenting to the proposal, or, at all events, offering no objection to the appointment of a commission by this government for the purpose of making an inquiry such as is asked for in this motion. I would like, for the sake of placing them upon the record, to read some of the resolutions which have been passed by the various bodies which I have mentioned. They are particularly pointed, and, to begin with, I would like to place before the House the resolution of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, which is in the following words:
Resolved, that inasmuch as the natural resources of Canada in its rivers, in its forests and in its farm lands-are of immeasurable extent and commercial value, and are urgently calling for the best and most approved means of development and utilization; and whereas the present methods of production require further scientific stimulus-more especially in the mechanical branches of a broadly ' national character, through a proper and special educational system; be it resolved, that this Trades and Labour Congress of Canada place itself on record as in favour of the establishment of industrial technical schools throughout the Dominion, and it is hereby an imperative instruction to the executive of this body to use its best efforts* at an early date, in urging the importance of the subject upon the serious attention ol the Dominion government with a view to the establishment of such a system of special education throughout Canada.
Then, the Trades and Labour Congress, in addition to the resolution which I have just read, have presented memorials to the government on more than one occasion in the same direction, and I quote from one

of the memorials which have been presented the following language:
The workmen of Canada are strongly of opinion that the welfare and development of Canada demand some large scheme of technical education. It is not a matter alone for the welfare of the workmen or of the employer, hut of the whole Canadian people. We want Canada to be foremost in the arts and manufactures, and we are just at that stage of industrial development when the institution of technical schools would be ot most value.
The Manufacturers' Association of Canada has passed a resolution very similar in terms to the resolution which I have just read, but I do not find that I have before me a copy of it, although it was quoted by me in the remarks which I made to the House in the session of 1907 and is upon ' Hansard.' The various boards of trade and chambers of commerce from the Atlantic to the Pacific have passed upon this question, but, without reading all the resolutions, I take that passed by the Halifax Board of Trade as a fair sample of the resolutions which have been passed by the other boards and chambers. It is in the following language:
Be it resolved, that in view of tlie facts that the foremost nations of the world have definitely proven that the technical education is the greatest weapon of modern industrial warfare, and that Canada's immense natural resources should be intelligently and efficiently developed by the most modern methods, and whereas, Canada owes it to Canadians to furnish them the technical training adequate jo _ carry on such development, that the Dominion government be requested to appoint an able commission of investigation to ascertain the best measures for establishing technical education in this Dominion of Canada.
I quote these various resolutions for the purpose of showing that the demand foi technical education is by no means local or sectional, but is entirely national in its character.
During the last thirty or forty years great changes have taken place in the educational methods of many of the older countries of the world. Notably is this the fact in the case of Germany, France, Holland, Belgium, Great Britain and the United States. Each of these countries has calmly sat down to consider its educational system, and each will be found to-day expending very large sums of money, not upon the old scholastic routine, but more particularly in looking after the actual needs of its great industrial classes for the purpose, in the first instance, of enabling the individual citizen the better to gain a livelihood, and, in the second place, for the purpose of enabling the nation itself to maintain its proper place in the markets of the world. The demand for technical education on the 33
part of the craftsman, the artisan and the workman of this country arises, no doubt, from the laudable desire of the mechanic to better himself in his own art or his own trade, in the hope thereby that he might increase his remuneration, and in the hope thereby that he might perform his work under less laborious conditions than hitherto. The demand for a system of technical education on the part of the employer or the manufacturer arises from the fact that in recent years the manufacturers of this country have from experience found that it is a difficult matter for them, either in the home market or in foreign markets, to compete against manufacturers of countries where there is a large staff of technically instructed artisans at their disposal.
I am well aware, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps the most formidable objection which *can be made to the proposal which I have the honour to lay before the House, will be the constitutional objection. The objection will be that under the constitution undeT which we in Canada are governed the whole question of education, by section 93 of the British North America Act, is a matter for the exclusive jurisdiction of the various provinces, and at first blush, upon a superficial examination of the question, that objection might be most formidable, indeed, might prove an absolute barrier to any action upon this subject by this House. However, I think that upon an examination of the Act and proper appreciation of what is meant by technical education the House will agree with me that there are many things that this parliament might do in regard to technical education which will in no way infringe upon the rights or the exclusive jurisdiction of the various provinces under section 93 of the British North America Act. Unfortunately, the term used, I think universally, in the English speaking world, to describe this particular kind of training, is technical education. A more correct phrase, to my mind, would be industrial training and probably, if the phrase were industrial training and not technical education, there would be less objection from the point of view of those who maintain that this is a matter now which infringes upon the right of the provinces in the matter of education. I am not positive that I can quote the exact language of section 93 of the British North America Act, but its provision generally is that, in regard to education the provinces shall have exclusive jurisdiction.
In answer to the objection upon the constitutional ground, I would state, in the first place, that one must consider the exact or precise meaning of the word 'education' as used in the 93rd section of the British North America Act. That Act was passed as far back as 1867. At that



time there was no such thing as technical education known within the confines of British America, and so technical education or industrial training did not enter into the contemplation of the men who framed that section. I submit that the word education as expressed in that section must receive its plain ordinary meaning, which is that course of instruction which we give to the youth of this country in the public schools, the high schools, the collegiate institutes and the universities; a training in languages, classics and moderns, in mathematics, in arts, in science and kindred subjects. It is entirely a scholastic training, one destined to turn out cultured and refined scholars in the Dominion, and that I submit is the meaning of the word education as used in the 93rd section. But technical.education is-an entirely different thing. It is a matter of economics rather than of culture; it is a matter of dollars and cents rather than of scholarship or refinement. That is the distinction I draw between the two, and in order to bring that distinction more plainly to the attention of the hon. members who hitherto have probably treated the subject with more or less indifference, let me place before the House the ordinary curriculum which is prescribed in the average institute of technology, whether it be in Europe, in Britain or in the United States. We all know the ordinary curricula of the colleges and universities of the countrv, but the curriculum of an institute of technology is an entirely different matter. In the average curriculum of a technical institute there will be a department of physics, including such subjects as light, heat, sound, electricity and magnetism; a department of hydrostatics treating of such things as liquids, gases, hydraulic engineering and machinery; a department of mechanics, treating of force, motion, gravitation and kindred subjects; a department of chemistry, where chemistry will be taught in all its branches, embracing theory and practical research; a department of mathematics, where mathematics will be taught so far as is required for practical application to scientific work; a department of free hand and industrial drawing and design; a department of machine construction and pattern making; a department of architectural design and decoration, clav modelling and leather cutting, and a complete course in mineralogy, metallurgy, geology, and engineering in all its branches.
Are not all these subjects now taught in the higher branches of education?

In a few institutions, yes. It may be argued that all the subjects I have enumerated are at the pres-Mr. GUTHRIE.
ent day taught in some way or other in the schools of the country. We know that the University of Toronto has its faculty of applied science, that McGill University has a very elaborate faculty of applied science, that Queens University has its department of mines, and that other universities are similarly equipped, so that it is possible for one to obtain instruction in almost any of the subjects I have enumerated at one or otheT of the great Canadian universities. But, Sir, that is accounted for by the fact that these universities have gone beyond what was the original intention of their founders; they have deemed it necessary in order to meet the needs of the people to go beyond the scholastic or academic training which in former years was considered sufficient. But, Sir, these institutions are only for the favoured few, and it is for that reason that I urge the view upon the House which I now do. The demand for technical education in Canada does not come from the children of parents who can give them a university education; it does not come from the rich, it comes from the moulder and the machinist, the metal workeT and the wood worker, the w eaver and the spinner, the shipwright and the millwright, the stonemason and the bricklayer. These are the men who are today making demands, not only upon this government but upon the provincial legislatures, for a more advanced system of industrial training.
Does the hon. gentleman pretend to argue that when the British North America Act was enacted these subjects were not included in the higher branches of education then?

I think I can say without fear of contradiction that every subject I have read to the House as part of the curriculum of an institute of technology, with the single exception of chemistry, would not be found in the ordinary curriculum of any Canadian university in 1867. These subjects have only been taught in the university course within 15 or 20 years at the most indeed it is only within the last ten years that faculties of applied science in our universities have become of any very great importance. But, my argument simply is that when the word education was placed in the British North America, Act it meant the scholastic training to which I have referred and it did not mean industrial training at all. But, another answer to any objections which may be taken upon constitutional grounds as against the federal government carrying into effect such a motion as I present, may fairly be found in the language of section 91 of the British North America Act. Section 91 prescribes among other things that in

matters concerning trade and commerce this parliament shall have jurisdiction, and I submit that the question of industrial training is really a matter pertaining to the trade and commerce of the Dominion. It vitally affects the trade and commerce of Canada, it vitally affects our manufactured product as to its quality, its quantity and its means of transportation. It also affects the question of obtaining foreign markets for our products and the prices to be obtained. Indeed the Department of Trade and Commerce is to-day carrying on what in the German empire is a distinct branch of their technical training, because our department is sending out trade agents to various parts of the world to secure trade and to make reports on trade conditions. I submit then that the . training meant by the term technical education is a matter which closely affects the commercial standing of the country, that it is a matter which this parliament might well deal with, and that it cannot be open to the objection that it comes within the term 'education' in section 93 and so belongs to the provinces. Let me submit a parallel case. At the city of Kingston we have the Royal Military College, where this government is actually engaged in the work of tuition. A general education is afforded in that institution. They teach mathematics, languages, English literature, general subjects. They give a man a good ail-round education apart entirely from military requirements. It may be asked, why does the government do that in the face of section 93 of the British North America Act? It is immediately answered that this is a matter of militia and defence, over which this government has exclusive jurisdiction. Might we not say the same of industrial training as related to the trade and commerce of the country? We engage in the work of tuition at Kingston simply as a sort of adjunct to militia and defence; why not engage in industrial training as an adjunct to our trade and commerce?
I think I may fairly ask the House to consider another answer to the argument that the adoption of this motion would be an encroachment upon the constitutional rights of the provinces of this Dominion, that is, that the question is of national concern, and not a local or sectional matter. Let us see how other countries have dealt with this question, and what they include under the term technical education. No other country so far as I know has a constitutional Act precisely similar to the British North America Act; but there are other countries in which are applied general principles very similar to those under which we live in Canada. Notably is this the case in Switzerland, where there is a federal authority with a number of autonomous cantonal governments. Notably also is this the case in the United States, under 33i
their federal system, with their state governments. I might also point to the great empire of Germany, which is made up of a great number of states or principalities, with a federal authority presiding over all. In each of these countries industrial training is looked on entirely as a national matter, not as a state or municipal matter, and not as a matter of education in the sense of scholarship.
Germany has been the great pioneer, the great _ progenitor, in this work. The first technical institute in Germany was established at Carlsruhe in 1825, another at Munich in 1827, another at Dresden in 1828, and another at Stuttgart in 1832. These were the pioneer schools of industrial training, no other country in the world having adopted the system up to that time. But the work that Germany started 85 years ago has spread enormously until to-dav it has the most complex system of industrial training known to the civilized world. That system is briefly as follows. They have their public schools very similar to those in this and other countries, and in connection with the public schools they have a system of manual training very similar to what we have in the public schools of Ontario and probably in those of other provinces. It is not with the manual training part of the work that my resolution deals. That may be looked on more as a matter of education in the strict sense of the word. Indeed, I do not think the Trades and Labour Congress is in favour of manual training, because it has a tendency to turn out on the country a great many unfinished mechanics. After the public school course has been taken by the Gerrnan youth, he selects his trade or occupation, and, as an apprentice, is eligible for entrance into one of the technical continuation schools. This is really the first step in his industrial training. There are something like 2,200 of these schools in Germany to-day, attended by over 325,000 pupils. After having taken a course in a continuation school, the pupil is eligible for entrance to a higher grade technical institute, or specialized trade school.
What is the length of that course?

It varies from two to three years consecutively, a great deal of the instruction being given at night. Some of the schools are free, and in some a small fee is charged. At the conclusion of that course, on which the German youth enters as an apprentice, he comes out as a more or less finished mechanic. But there is a much higher grade in the specialized trade schools, to which he then becomes eligible. In Germany there are 524 of these, subdivided as follows:	Schools of mechanics,
25; schools of mining, 58; schools of architecture and construction, 53; schools of

metallurgy, 10; schools of textiles, 117; schools of wood-carving, 24; schools of industrial art and design, 27; schools of ocean navigation, 41; schools of fresh water navigation, 52; schools of shipbuilding, 5. According to the curriculum of an ordinary building trade school, we find that a man who is otherwise looked on as a very good mechanic is taught there, stone-cutting and laying, brick making, plastering, carpentry, scientific construction, uses, strength and value of materials, designing, modelling and ornamentation, heating and ventilation, road and bridge building, drainage and irrigation. In that whole curiculum there is not a single subject that one would say *came within the definition of the word education as used in the 93rd section of the British North America Act. The course of instruction in a textile school covers the whole process from the lowest grade of primary weaving to textile and mechanical engineering. This is taught not only in the 117 textile schools, but also in 8 universities. The course including weaving, spinning, bleaching, dyeing, machinery, properties of raw materials, manufacturing of all woven and all spun materials. In the curriculum of one of these textile schools there is no subject taught that one could argue came within the meaning of the word education as used in the 93rd section of our Constitutional Act. Take the curriculum of the art trade school and these schools are schools of the highest consequence. They are not schools in the strict sense of the word, but deal more with commercial art, more with ornamentation and design. The courses there consist of drawing, modelling, ornamentation, painting, furniture designing, wood carving, pottery and leather cutting. These are the highest classes of trade schools, but in addition they have in Germany nine technical universities and three technical mining universities.
Axe there stated courses in these schools?

I do not know the length of time. I have not come across that in my researches, but I fancy there must be some stated .time and system of examination. To show the length to which the -system has been carried in Germany, take the Principality of Wurtemburg, with a less population than Ontario, and you will find that in Wurtemburg there is one state university, one technical school, one textile school, one mechanical school, one building trades school, three weaving schools, two hundred and thirty-one industrial improvement schools, eighteen domestic schools for women, a commercial college and an agricultural high school. And all these are in but one state or province of the German empire, with a population less than that of Ontario. That great institute of technol-Mr. GUTHRIE.
-ogy instituted at Berlin and maintained entirely by the empire itself-the Berlin Royal Technical College-has 140 professors, 260 assistants, 3,500 students, and gives courses in engineering, chemistry, metallurgy, and there are besides free museums, free art galleries and free laboratories. The expenditure on technical education and industrial training in Germany amounts to a tremendous sum annually.
One question for us to consider is how is the cost of all these met? These are maintained according to the following contributions: Tuition fees constitute 23 per cent of the cost, municipal grants for school funds and other donations 49 per cent, and the German empire itself contributes 28 per cent. I mention this to show that in the empire of Germany, the question of industrial training is looked at as a great national undertaking and not as a local matter at all.
Are these schools all under the control of the empire or of the individual states?	-

I cannot inform my hon. friend on that point, but from such facts as have been brought before me, I think the control rests with the municipalities, though with regard to some universities, not only are they [DOT]controlled but they are maintained to the extent of 28 per cent by the empire.
It may be asked what has that system resulted in? In the first place it has resulted in furnishing a population with a larger percentage of highly skilled artisans than can be found in any other country. It has resulted in transferring some of the trade heretofore enjoyed by other countries to the German empire. Its results can be found in the records of the manufacture of aniline dyes. Twenty-five years ago the dye stuffs of the- whole world were manufactured in Great Britain. To-day the dye stuffs of the whole world are manufactured in Germany. This is one of the direct results of the work of the German students in the technical laboratories of the German empire. So with the coal tar products. Today Germany controls the whole trade in these products, and the reason is that she has discovered improved processes through the researches in her laboratories. In textiles, the German trade became so enormous about 1890 that the merchants and manufacturers of Great Britain, ^ at^ their own expense, appointed a commission to inquire into the conditions and discover the reason for the increase in German trade and the diminution in their own. That commission reported that the reason was to be found in the improved machinery, methods and higher standing of the German mechanical workman. And that report being submitted to the trade at Manchester,

steps were at once taken to institute technical education, and a scheme has gradually been developed, not only in Manchester, but in other parts of Great Britain.
So in the iron and steel trade. Twenty-five years ago the British exports of manufactured iron and steel were five and six times as great as those of Germany. Today, according to a recent article in the London ' Financial News,' German exports are almost on a par with those of England, and it is pointed out that raw material is more expensive in Germany than in England. According to this article, wages are higher perhaps in Germany than in England, and yet the German trade in iron and steel is rapidly equalling that of Great Britain. What is the reason? It is not to be found in the tariff legislation of either country but in the greater skill and improved methods of Germany arising from the development of her system of industrial training.
Turn for a moment to Switzerland as a fair example. It is made up of a number of cantons, with a federal government and constitution somewhat similar to our own In 1901 Switzerland spent, in round numbers, a million francs on technical education; 75 per cent was contributed by the various cantons and 25 per cent by the federal government.
Let us take a glance at the United States. Up to 1862 they did little or nothing with regard to technical education. During that year Congress passed an Act which provided that a substantial land grant should be given each state which would establish colleges with special courses in agriculture and mechanical arts. This offer was taken advantage of by many of the states. The State of New York received a land grant of some 800,000 acres, Pennsylvania 700,000 acres, Ohio 400,000, and other states lesser quantities. The Act was supplemented in 1890 by an Act which provided that each of the states which had established colleges, with these particular courses in agriculture and the mechanical arts, should receive a cash grant of $15,000 for the year 1890, and an additional grant of $1,000 for each succeeding year until the grant for each particular college should reach the sum of $25,000. That system of land grant and money grant has been in operation since that day, with the result that the federal government of the United States has paid in cash to such colleges the sum of $15,000,000 in round numbers and has given land grants aggregating about $16,000,000. The cash grant paid last year by the federal government of the United States to such colleges was about $2,500,000. What has that resulted in? It has resulted in the establishment of about sixty technical schools or colleges. In 44 of these colleges, courses are provided in mechanical engineering; in
38, in electrical engineering; in 37, in civil engineering; in 21, in mining engineering; in 6, in architecture; in 4, in metallurgical, technical and railway engineering. It is true that in all these cases where money has been granted by the federal authority in the United States, it has been to some college or state university where these courses were added to the ordinary courses of the university for the purpose, no doubt, of obtaining the land or money grant; but that does not affect the question and viewed from a constitutional point, it is of no importance whether the institute of technology be by itself or be an adjunct of a college or a university. If we undertook to establish it in Canada purely and simply as a matter of industrial training, it would not be necessary in any sense of the word-

Are you aware that in the Act making these appropriations the federal government say:
Nothing in this Act shall interfere with the right of the state to deal with this particular matter.
-acknowledging in full the state's right of control.
I was not aware of that, but I think it would be a very reasonable provision, and I am sure that no state or province would object to such federal grant.
The federal grant does not interfere with the autonomy of the state.

I think we might adopt some safeguard of that kind in this country. We find to-day that industrial training has been inaugurated practically all over the eastern and middle states of America. The New England states are full of technical institutes, and they have been of great benefit to American industry. One recent achievement in the schools of Massachusetts has been in regard to Canadian wool, which had for many years been regarded as a coarse wool fit only for the manufacture of blankets and carpets. Not long ago I had occasion to discuss this question and the question of leather goods with a man from Massachusetts who told me that, through the work carried on in one of the technical institutes in Massachusetts, it was found that the coarse wool of Canada could be used to a very large extent in the manufacture of the best quality of tweed and worsted they are producing in the United States, and Canadian wool is now being used in the proportion of about 70 per cent to 30 per cent of other wools and other materials in the manufacture of these high class cloths. That is one result, perhaps a minor one, of a system of industrial training and industrial investigation.

In Great Britain practically nothing was done in reference to industrial training until the Manchester manufacturers and merchants took the matter up in 1891 in the manner I have outlined. In the next year the British goverment appointed a commission to visit Germany and the United States, and I think France and Belgium, for the purpose of acquiring the fullest possible information in regard to industrial training. The result of these inquiries was that the question of industrial training attracted the attention of the great manufacturers of Great Britain and a large number of very successful technical institutes have been established there and are attended by a large number of workmen. Indeed, some British manufacturers have gone the length of offering bonuses to their workmen to take a course in some one or other of these technical institutes. One result of this movement on the part of Great Britain came to my attention recently in discussing this question with the same man who gave me the information on the question of wool. He said that until recently the United States was certainly supreme in regard to the manufacture of boots and shoes. They not only supplied their own market, but largely the Canadian market and very largely the British market. He said that recently British manufacturers of boots and shoes have been making articles of a quality that will sell in the United States and certain consignments have .come in and have been sold in the United States. How was that done? That was done by the British manufacturer bringing from the United States certain American machinery, American processes of manufacture and American lasts, placing them in Great Britain, teaching the work in some one or other of the technical institutes of Great Britain and producing an article which resembles in appearance to all intents and purposes, the American shoe, but is of a superior quality. My information on that subject came about a year ago from a man from Massachusetts and I notice in this morning's newspaper that the editor of the Toronto ' Globe ', speaking before the Canadian Club at Ottawa on Saturday, referred to this same question of the manufacture of leather goods from Great Britain being sold in the United States, this information having been gained last summer in Great Britain, mine having come from a man residing in Massachusetts. Information coming from two points so diverse is, I think, probably reliable. The change that has taken place in the shoe trade is certainly to be attributed to the courses of technical training which the British workman has undergone in one or other of the technical institutes of Great Britain.
May I point to one other answer which I think is a complete reply to any objection Mr. GUTHRIE.
that might be raised on constitutional grounds, and that is that the Dominion government has already to a considerable extent entered upon the field of industrial training and that so far no objection has been raised. In regard to agriculture, we have established a system of technical education under this government in the experimental farm that is conducted here in Ottawa. Many of the institutes of Germany and some of the United States which are purely and simply technical institutes, do nothing more than what is done at the experimental' farm here. They carry on experiments as to new and improved machinery and as to new processes, they issue bulletins and in that way inform the public upon these various matters-just the work that is being carried on at the experimental farm. That is certainly a work of instruction, and if you like, a work of education. It is educating Canadian farmers, it is done for that purpose and has had the effect of raising the standard of farming very greatly throughout the Dominion of Canada. What this motion asks is that this government will do in regard to manufacturers, or with regard to our natural resources, just what it has been and is doing with regard to agriculture. It is carrying on technical work, it is engaged in technical education in regard to agriculture, and we ask that the same principles precisely be applied to other natural resources of Canada, and also to the manufactured products of Canada. I mention also the work of education which we are carrying on at the Royal Military College at Kingston to-day. We are carrying on also work at the School of Navigation at Kingston, teaching the science of navigation. That is a technical work, and in the German empire they have a large number of schools specially appointed for the work of teaching navigation pure and simple which this government has engaged in. Then we have two marine biological research stations carrying on work at Gaspe and on the Georgian Bay. This government, through the Intercolonial railroad, is indirectly providing for educational work at the University of McGill; the Intercolonial railway makes an annual grant to the Faculty of 'Applied Science of McGill University for carrying on experiments and work in testing different materials. That is an indirect contribution of this parliament to the University of McGill College. Then we are carrying on extensive experiments and a good deal of research work under Prof. Haanel. He has been investigating various ways of smelting Canadian ores. That is the very work which is taught 'at all the greater technical institutes in Germany and the United States. He has been engaged recently in carrying on experiments with a view of rendering the large and valuable peat lands of Ontario of some value. That

is a work of technical education and technical investigation, which we ask should be continued. Those are works which the Dominion government is carrying on to-day, and carrying on successfully for the good of the people. We ask that the work be continued.
In what way would you suggest? I have not at my disposal or within my knowledge all the avenues in which the government might put forth some effort, but I think it certainly could make money grants to institutions that are carrying on this work.
I think they could, as the German empire has done, establish experimental stations and museums throughout Canada, where the work might be carried on with new and improved machinery, in new and improved processes of manufacture. They might carry their investigations further in regard to electrical smelting, and the treatment of all native Canadian ores. They might carry on successfully serious experiments in regard to the great pulpwood growth of this country, in the way of seeing how this could be rendered a greater national asset than it is now, how that could be best manufactured and best transported. They could carry further their investigation, particularly in regard to naval construction and architecture. This is a mater which . has been taken up very largely by Germany. Germany has five ship-building schools and about 100 navigation schools; whereas twenty-five years ago it had none. It is now building a number of its own craft, twenty-five years ago it did not build any. That is an achievement in Germany also due most directly to the result of technical education and training.
I know it is sometimes skid that this is a matter which only pertains to a few of the larger cities, perhaps, and to bodies of workmen in those various cities. But I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in the villages and towns of this country there is a tremendous demand for opportunity on the part of our workingmen to improve themselves in the various trades and crafts. Time was not so many years ago when a certain institution in the United States, called the Scranton Correspondence School, was looked upon as more or less of a, joke, as one of those sharp Yankee money making concerns which, by expensive advertising, would be able to gull the public and rake in the people's money. However, from what I know of that institution in Scranton, it is by no means a joke, and while it is a very successful commercial undertaking, and pays most handsome dividends, it has disseminated a tremendous amount of valuable information, not only in the United States, but in Canada. I was surprised to hear from a man interested in that school, that last year it drew from Canadian workingmen and artisans nearly
$800,000 in fees for tuition, and from the city of Montreal alone last year over $100,000. That money was drawn directly from the pockets of mechanics and artisans in this_ country, from men who were endeavouring by all means in their power to secure what is necessary to give them perfect knowledge of their craft, and who have no opportunity either to go to McGill, or the University of Toronto, where schools in science are certainly afforded to the children of the rich. I am glad to say that in Montreal an institution of technology has been founded. I believe that when it is at work it will have the effect immediately of keeping that $100,000 of the workmen and mechanics of Montreal within the city of Montreal instead of sending it over to the Scranton School of Correspondence and others. The Scranton school is only one of many schools; but it is the most prominent of those in the United States, and has been the subject of a special report by the British commission who went thoroughly into the institutions in the United States. I am glad also that in Nova Scotia a very large institution has been opened, and work is to be carried on there, I trust, on a very large scale. In Ontario, too, something has been done. But if we compare what has been done by any of the provinces of Canada with what has been accomplished in the little principality of Wurtemburg, we can see in a moment what is yet to be done in Canada in regard to this great question.
Now I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the passage of a motion like this cannot in any way prejudice the right or interest of any provincial authority. If such a commission were appointed, a small commission of five or six capable men, to visit Great Britain, and several European countries, and the United States, the expense involved would not be considerable. If it should turn out as a result of their investigation that there is nothing which this parliament could do in the way of furthering the great cause of industrial training, we will know it; that is one thing. But if the information will be of value to the various provinces of Canada, the money will not be lost, and I am personally satisfied that there are a great many things this government can do. I have not sufficient time to enumerate them, but I simply place before the House such facts as I have been able to gain from conversation, from the ordinary means of research. I know that I am but poorly equipped to discuss the question intelligently as it should be discussed. I sincerely hope that some other hon. members will continue the debate, as I know that there are those in this House who are well aware of all the facts and all the circumstances, and far better able to discuss the subject than I am.

I am sure, Mr.'Speaker, that this House is under a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) for the able address he has just delivered. It is rich with information and replete with reasonings, conclusive reasonings, it seems to me, in affirmation of the proposition laid down in this resolution. 1 think this is one of the best things that have emanated from the other side of the House this session, perhaps because it was not inspired by a Liberal caucus or by a Liberal government. I have great pleasure in paying a personal compliment to the hon. gentleman who has brought this matter before the House. If this resolution were amended as suggested and instead of the word ' technical education ' the words ' industrial training ' were inserted I think it would better meet the occasion. As to the jurisdiction of this House, it has been said, and truly, that this parliament is doing to-day for the farmers what we are asking it to do for the industrial population. We are, by our experimental farms and by the machinery and efforts of the Department of Agriculture, acquiring information which is being used by the different agricultural colleges and other institutions. Even the public schools which are under the control of the provinces are availing themselves of this knowledge. In Belgium, Switzerland, Germany and all the old;r countries, they are doing this work of sheer necessity. For centuries their natural resources have been developed and their increase of wealth and importance come from the work of the hand and the brain. In our country it is perhaps different at the present time. The farmer, the merchant, the holder of bonds, the possessor of property finds, without any individual effort on his own part, that, by reason of the development going on around him, his possessions in four or five years have doubled in value. We may expect greater results if this question is taken up at the present time. If we can make one acre of the farmer's land produce what an acre and a half formerly yielded, if we can make two pairs of hands do the work formerly done by three pairs, that adds so much to the general wealth of the country. A trained industrial people is one of the best assets that any country can have, and if I were to look for some phrase to illumine or brighten this thought I would take the words of Whittier who, when paying a tribute to his own -state, does not refer to the visible or latent wealth of the forest, the field or the mine, to the accumulation of capital or to the vast volume of commerce, but he savs that:
The riches of the commonwealth Are clear, strong minds and hearts of health: Mr. GUTHRIE.
And more to her than gold or gain,
The cunning hand and cultured brain.
I do not think there will be any objection from the different provinces on the score that this parliament is exceeding its jurisdiction. If the parliament is animated by the spirit of the people of Winnipeg, the city which I have the honour to represent, I am sure that its action will meet with the approval of the people generally. The city of Winnipeg has dumped down upon it a large foreign population. There are something like fifty or sixty languages spoken there, and the people of Winnipeg have established night schools during the winter season at a cost of thousands of dollars to themselves. There was nothing to compel them to do that, but they are satisfied to do it and there is no objection to it on the part of the citizens although it considerably increases the taxes. This motion does not commit the House to the principle of technical education or to any other principle. All it asks for is a commission of inquiry, a commission composed of the most competent men entirely clear of politics to get all the information available upon the subject and if they gain that information, whether in Europe, or Massachusetts, or in any other place, it will be available for the benefit of all the province and every educational institution in the different provinces of the Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) that my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has made one of the most important contributions to the discussions of this House that has ever been made in my experience as a member and that he has dealt with a subject second to none in relation to the industrial and commercial development of this country. He has given us a very exhaustive explanation of technical education and of its application in the older European countries. He has given us some very exhaustive and lengthy reasons and arguments why technical education, so-called, should not be read into the conditions of the constitution which provides that authority with respect to education shall remain in the hands of the provinces.
I want to emphasize those reasons and perhaps my hon. friend will permit me to add a few more practical reasons why this government should be prepared to take up this question as set forth in this resolution, appoint this commission, provide an appropriation and control the technical education of this country. I can quite understand how the government will be naturally cautious before taking upon itself financial responsibility which constitutional authority may declare legitimately was intended to belong to the provinces. When we consider the extent of this country, the enormous cost of its development in matters

appertaining exclusively to the authority of the Dominion parliament that the provinces cannot manage for Canada, I do not blame the Dominion authority for exercising some little care before it takes increased responsibility in reference to expenditures upon questions of education. But, I agree entirely with my hon. friend from South Wellington that the question of technical education is not associated or related to the question of general education, which, in my opinion, was placed by the constitution under the exclusive control of the provinces. My hon. friend made reference to two or three kinds of industrial training. He referred to the manual training schools and to the system of technical education. Considerable confusion has existed in the minds of some people as to the difference between these classes of education. I only know them as they exist in England and I noticed, as my hon. friend pointed out, that the labour organizations of this country had declared by resolution that they were opposed to any system of manual training, because a system ol manual training turned out mechanics who were brought into competition with the ordinary artisans of the country. My hon. friend presented a resolution from an important body of men. Trade schools, as they exist in England, are schools that take the place of the old system of apprenticeship. The system of apprenticeship in England was based upon a contract between the man who owned a business and the son of some other man to the effect that the apprentice would confine himself to this man's business for a given number of years. The system of trade schools was inaugurated in England as a substitute for the apprenticeship system and in these schools young men are taught the specialties of a particular trade. If a man wants to be a carpenter he is instructed in these trade schools in everything that appertains to that calling and so it is with respect to all other trades. I want to put myself on record as being entirely opposed to the conclusion of anybody or organization of la-bourmen who would object to a system of manual training.
Some horn MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I go further and I say that I am astonished that any organization of labour men should oppose any system of education. In doing so they evince the very spirit that prompted certain classes of wealthy Englishmen, sixty or seventy years ago, to oppose in the British parliament appropriations of money for the advancement of education. These wealthy Englishmen proclaimed that it would be a serious disadvantage if the rural communities were educated, and there are yet men living in England who made the statement on the floor of the House
of Commons that if the artisans of England had a knowledge of history and science then representative government would be in danger. I say, Sir, that the spirit which actuated these men of the classes in England to restrict the intelligence of the masses is the self same spirit which prompts a labour organization to seek to restrict manual training in this country. Why ! above all others, labour men ought to stand for everything which conducts to developing the intelligence of the great masses of the community. A few years ago Andrew Carnegie gave a contribution of $50,000 to the city of Ottawa for a library, and the labour associations of this city passed resolutions against accepting that contribution for the reason that they declared the money was gained from the blood and sweat of the men whom Carnegie employed in his mills. At that time I wrote a letter to the Citizen over my own signature repudiating that contention and I held that if the tyrannies which makes it possible for capitalisits to secure unreasonable divisions of the profits of a business is ever to be subdued it can only be subdued by increasing the intelligence and knowledge of the workingmen and using such donations as that given by Carnegie towards that end. I am opposed to all kinds of restrictions, and when it comes to restricting the intelligence of my fellow men I am its avowed and open enemy.
Now, I want to give the government two or three practical reasons why they should support this resolution and appoint the commission which it asks for. My first reason has been expressed by my hon. friend from Winnipeg, and it is because technical training contributes to the development of the country, to its increased wealth, and to the protection of its citizens. My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) said th it technically trained artisans were the greatest asset of any country, and let me add that no country in the world to-day is suffering a greater disadvantage in the development of its resources than is Canada because of this. She has to come into competition in the open markets of the world with the older nations who have workingmen trained under high class systems of technical education, and Canada has to draw her supplies not from the men who are the most technical in the old countries, but generally speaking from the men who are denied the same high educational advantages in this country. When I think of the rapid development of our country and when I see the few facilities for industrial training that we have, it has been a great surprise to me how our large industrial concerns and especially the railways, have ever managed to equip themselves with the number of trained men

required to carry on their enterprise. On the railways of Canada you have ashighly trained men as are to be found in any craft, and considering the numbers necessary to cope with the extensive development of our railway system it has always been a surprise to me how the railways managed to procure the trained labour required. Now, it is a well established fact that the value of a product increases with the increased intelligence of the workman, and perhaps the noblest and certainly the most profitable contribution we could make to the welfare of our people would be the expenditure of public money for the purpose of increasing the intelligence of our craftsmen. That is the purpose of this resolution. Another thing which concerns us very intimately is the providing of increased safety for our industrial classes, and this can most effectually be done by affording them technical education in their particular calling. In this connection I shall make special reference to the coal mining industry on the Pacific coast. It is deplorable to think that the highest percentage of mine accidents in any country is to be found in Canada, and the province of British Columbia, I regret to say, is lamentably pre-eminent in that respect. I should sav in justice to my friends from Nova Scotia who are largely interested in coal mining that the accidents in their mines are relatively fewer than in the mines of British Columbia. Now, the explanation for that condition of things in Canada	is	that	a large	number	ofmen without training are employed in working jthe mines. We have been startled	in	the	last few	months	by
accounts of explosions in coal mines; sometime ago there was one near Nanaimo, and just a few days ago 300 men were buried in an Illinois mine. Now, the royalties from the mines go to the provincial revenue and the supervision of mines lies with the province; but in the United States the geological department has extended its authority over the operation of coal mines and whenever serious accidents occur there the federal government sends their technical officers to make investigation and to find the cause. The history of mining and mining accidents in England shows that it is the scientific men who discover the *causes of these accidents. The Dominion government has a Mining Department with its technical officers, and I want to suggest to mv hon. friend the Minister of Mines that whenever a mining accident occurs in any part of this country one of those technical officers be sent to investigate the cause of the accident. Let me mention one or two mining accidents that occurred in British Columbia, the causes of which are not likely to be discovered by the ordinary practising engineer. The accident at the Mr. RALPH SMITH.
Fernie coal mine was due to a freak in the geological formation, which could only be discovered and remedied by scientific technical men who understand the business of mining. In England they have had very many explosions in mines, just as we have in British Columbia, and they have never been certain that they have found the real causes of these explosions.
Let me bring to the attention of the House another matter which has a very practical bearing on this question. Some months ago we were startled by the great number of accidents that occurred in the handling of dynamite in the construction of the Grand Trunk railway. Have we ever endeavoured to discover the cause of these accidents? In my opinion there is just one answer. In the first place, we have not the technically trained men who understand how to handle high explosives, and in the next place, we have no testing plant in Canada to enable even intelligent workmen to learn the properties of these high explosives. This is a matter that should be taken up by the Mining Department of the government. If we consider the practical importance of that department, it seems to me impossible for the government to avoid the responsibility of providing for technical education along these lines. Let us consider what the government has been doing. It has discovered from experience that it is impossible to avoid technical education in connection with the operations of certain departments. My hon. friend mentioned the Marine Department with its schools of navigation. The scope of these schools must constantly expand with the growth of the Dominion. My hon. friend also referred to the educational work of the Department of Agriculture. The lands in the settled parts of this country are owned by the provinces, and the revenues derived from them go to the provinces; and yet this government, on its own initiative, has established a very important system of agricultural education in the form of experimental farms, farming and dairy schools, and especially in the circulation of lectures that have been given by scientific men connected with the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa. I venture to say from my experience that there is nothing more appreciated to-day by the people of the west than the scientific agricultural literature distributed by the Dominion government. I do not believe it is possible to have the results of the technical education provided by the several provinces of this Dominion distributed throughout this large country unless it is done by the Dominion authorities. For instance, Nova Scotia has a technical school of mining at Halifax. It is to the credit of Nova Scotia that it has done so much along this line. As a matter of fact, Nova Scotia has practically supplied the mining engineers

for the Dominion. My hon. friend referred to the correspondence schools. Although British Columbia is a mining province, it has no institution for technical training in mining, and but for the correspondence schools of the United States, we could not have had a sufficient number of mining engineers for the mining operations of the province. The mining engineer who wants to advance in his profession, must of necessity increase his knowledge by means of these schools, Let me say also that this system of education is not central, it is one which has to be distributed. It has to be taken to the door of the men who labour. My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said that they only began this system of technical education in England in 1892. Let me say this, that 30 or 35 years ago the British government had a science and art department and spent thousands of pounds sending scientific lecturers all over the country, and let me add that the mining engineers of that country to-day are men who took advantage of these lectures. Further, 30 years ago there was a thorough system of technical education in the way of university lecture courses in the old country. The "head men in the universities were distributed all over England to give lecture courses in technical matters and their expenses were to a large extent met by voluntary subscription.
My hon. friend has said a great deal about Germany, and no one will be disposed to undervalue the technical educational system of that country. But we know that the whole system of education there is part of their colossal militarism. Personally I prefer the free English system to the German. In Germany every man is compelled by the state to take advantage of the education provided, but I doubt very much that the German system has raised the mechanic and artisan of that country above the capacity of the British artisan. I have not yet been convinced that the system of educational training in Germany has done more for the workman than the British system has done for the British workman. But whatever system we adopt, it must be brought to the door of the ordinary workingman. You cannot expect a working man to leave his work at Vancouver in order to take up a university course elsewhere. Any system of education, to be useful to the industrial classes, must be distributed, so that the people can avail themselves of it without detriment to their daily work. Any system of education should provide for the sending out of lecturers all over the country. That could be done now by the Department of Mining. Scientific trained men could be sent out to the mining centres all over Canada to give lectures in the different mining schools.
I think sufficient has been said to induce the government to take advantage of this resolution and provide a good appropriation by means of which important evidence may be collected on this subject, and the Dominion authority is the only one which can make the information thus collected profitable to every part of this Dominion.

The House is, I am . sure, very much indebted to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) for the very able speech he has made on this important question. I was very much interested also in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) and those of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Smith). I do not rise for the purpose of discussing the question of technical education itself. I assume that every hon. gentleman here is convinced that the question is one of the greatest importance to the Dominion, and it ought not to be necessary to say anything in favour of technical education at this stage in our history. My object in rising is to point out, in a few words, that the desire to have something done in this line by the federal authorities is not a local one, that it is not confined to the province of Ontario or British Columbia, or Manitoba, but that it exists in eastern Canada as well as the west. It is certainly not a new question in the province from which I have the honour to come. Some years ago I had the privilege of acting as chairman of a committee of the local legislature in that province appointed to investigate and report to the local government on this question, which has been a live one in Nova Scotia for a good many years. Some 15 or 20 years ago, when our present Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) was premier of that province, the demand arose that something should be done in the way of training the miners who were operating the coal mines. In answer to that demand, the local government established mining schools in the various industrial mining centres. These schools have been in operation ever since and have done very good work. Some 300 men have graduated from them and now occupy important positions of trust in the mines, not only of our own province, but of other provinces as well, and the United States.
Later on the fruit growers thought that something should be done for them, and an agricultural school was established in the Annapolis valley. That was carried on some years and then merged into the provincial agricultural college at Truro. That college has done splendid work. Some three or four hundred men trained there, go but that it exists in eastern Canada as and spread the knowledge gained in that

college among the farmers of the maritime provinces. There is no expense by the local government which has given better results than the money spent on the agricultural college at Truro.
But after the industrial expansion at Sydney, Amherst, New Glasgow and other places, it was felt something further should be done and two years ago, the Nova Scotia legislature devoted the large sum of $100,000 for the establishment of a technical school. The building has been erected and the college has been opened, and I trust it is doing good work.
I mention these facts to show that the subject of technical education is one which has taken deep root in the eastern as well as in the central provinces and the west. The technical school established at Halifax has formed branches throughout all the industrial centres of the province, and they are working together and no doubt will show very beneficial results. I might add that the progress which has been made is not confined to Nova Scotia. Similar good work is being done in Ontario. We all know that the agricultural college of Guelph has turned out men who have been of great benefit, not only to Ontario, but to every other province. We have some of those men in Nova Scotia. One of them is the principal of our agricultural college there and he is one of whom neither the college nor his province need in any way be ashamed. The Royal Military College at Kingston is also doing technical work and the McGill university students are known the world over. McGill university has earned a great reputation as a school of technical education. But, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend from South Wellington, these larger universities, such as Toronto and McGill, are only for the sons of rich men who can afford to send them to the city to attend the regular courses and spend two or three years in training, but are not open to the general run of people, and the want is keenly felt for something to be done in a general way.
The mover of the motion has pointed out what has been done in Germany. Something also has been done in France, Austria, Sweden and even in Russia and also in Great Britain. The people of Great Britain were a little slow to take up the idea. It was not until the prestige of their industrial establishments was threatened to some extent by Germany and others that they did adopt it. But good work is now being done in Great Britain in this line. There is no country in the world to-day which needs technical education no much as Canada. It is not money we require for the development of our country so much as men. We want in every department captains of industry who can take hold of our undeveloped resources and turn them into wealth. We are about to embark on the Mr. SINCLAIR.
construction of a Canadian navy and I will venture to say that the great difficulty the government will meet will not be the question of money, although money is always a serious question as the Finance Minister will tell you, but the question of men, of trained men to build these ships, to lay down plans, to make the models and turn them out as they ought to be turned out. This will be the most difficult question the government will have to meet. A few years ago we were all humiliated at the inception of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to find that the skilled men were imported from the United States. It may not have been absolutely necessary to do this but it was done to a very large extent in order to inaugurate that great enterprise. It will not again be found necessary to do this because we have now a considerable number of trained men among ourselves. The same thing happened at Sydney when the industrial expansion took place there. We had not a sufficient number of trained men and had to import them from a foreign country in order to start the steel works. I would suggest that something in the nature of the Morel Act be adopted in Canada, some scheme by which the local and municipal governments would contribute perhaps the largest share to this kind of education, the central government contributing a stated amount in cases where the local governments came up to a certain standard. I see no reason, under the circumstances, why that should not be done. I hope the government will take it into their serious consideration and that some forward movement will take place in regard to this very important matter.
