House resumed at eight o'clock.

I would like to say a word or two in support of this resolution before it is finally dealt with. I desire to preface my remarks by congratulating the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) who moved this resolution, both upon the resolution itself and upon the able manner in which he supported it. I am quite aware that the matter is not without difficulties if it is to be dealt with by the government, because it is a matter that calls for the expenditure of money, not a large sum, but still an expenditure of money along the lines of what is in a sense, at least, education. Now the fact that this question is of an educational nature has been mentioned as presenting a difficulty in the way of the federal government dealing with it. But I think that difficulty has been largely met by the hon. member who moved this resolution, and by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) and

others who have spoken. In a sense it is not a matter of education, using the word in a narrow sense, but it is a matter of practical training, of industrial training, in technical knowledge. There is no occasion to use the word ' education ' in this resolution at all. It seems to me something apart altogether from education as the word is ordinarily used, even if it were necessary to differentiate the matter in that way.
As has been pointed out to-day, the government in years gone by has undertaken to deal with matters that are no less matters of education than this. For instance, the attention which the government devotes to agriculture has been referred to, and the sums spent on agriculture have been mentioned as a precedent for government action in relation to this case. Certainly the government has spent large sums of money in what is practically the education of the farming class all over Canada, a work which is carried on by the Department of Agriculture. Now I have no complaint to make with the government on that score. But this matter of technical training is to the mechanic and the artisan what agricultural training and the agricultural college are to the student of agriculture and to farmers' sons. I believe the government has undertaken the work of education in several other branches of public affairs in this country. For instance, the military college at Kingston has been referred to, and the instruction given by the government in marine navigation and the examination of candidates for various departments in navigation. So there are to-day abundant precedents for legislation along the lines of what we are now discussing.
But that is not the only instance relevant to the question of whether it is one within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces; because, as has been pointed out by the mover of the resolution, the object sought to be attained is primarily the appointment of a commission to take evidence. Even if the government acted upon that suggestion and issued a commission, and then chose afterwards, in accordance with the recommendations of that commission, to go further and embark on an expenditure of money for the purpose, it could still be done in conjunction and in connection with the various provinces or municipalities in different parts of Canada, whose moneys or other assets could be joined with federal assistance. So that, even if it were a matter of education, it need not be taken out of the domain of provincial control, because it could be dealt with primarily as a matter of education by the provinces, assisted by some substantial contribution on the part of the Dominion government. So that difficulty, if it be one, could be got over.
But -what this resolution asks for is simply that a commission be appointed.
Now if the government did no more than appoint that commission to take evidence, the commission would probably report its evidence and findings, it would bring down to this House its recommendations, and even if the government went no further, they would be doing a large measure of substantial justice in this matter. We know that in various provinces action is being taken along the lines of this resolution, and if every province were to act in turn and issue just as many commissions as we have provinces, it would mean looking at the subject from so many different points of view, and if followed by legislation it would mean probably legislation of various kinds, showing a want of harmony and of breadth of view in dealing with a matter which requires some broad and comprehensive scheme. Now this is not education in a primary sense, because, as we all know, the provinces have undertaken that work. Time was when the state did not consider it a duty to educate the youth of a country; that period has happily long since passed, and no sane man would to-day for a moment suggest that it was not a proper and essential thing for the state to educate the youth. But there has arisen a need of what may be called secondary education, an education that has already been undertaken by many modern civilized countries, and that is the kind of education we are now considering. It is an education that is needed to fit the youth for the business of life, and this secondary education at the present time is given freely and unstintedly by every important country of Europe, and very largely by Great Britain. One would think that the time had come in this country when we could not afford to lag behind Europe. We are accustomed to refer to certain parts of southern Europe as being backward and unprogressive, but those countries are far ahead of us in this matter, they have solved the problems of technical education in a way that those countries find highly satisfactory. As has been pointed out this afternoon, some of the European countries have undertaken specially to deal with particular trades or callings, and in that way such trade or calling is dealt with in the most efficient manner possible. The days of apprenticeship are past, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Nanaimo, and an age has succeeded by which the state has intervened and assumed the burden of what was formerly performed by the master to the employee. Technical education is engaging the attention of every large city in Canada. These communities naturally look to the government for something to guide them in putting into actual practice this method of education. They naturally look, to the government to provide them with the very latest knowledge available on this very important

question. It is too much to expect that municipalities, even if they be large cities like Toronto and Montreal, will go on a meandering trip around the world to find the latest system of technical education, and they are looking to this central government to take the first steps along the line of at least supplying them with all available information on this question. We have some technical education in Toronto, but it is of the higher order, being in connection with the University of Toronto. But, the hoard of education in Toronto is dealing with this matter. It is considering a question of the establishment of technical schools as an adjunct to the common school education in that city, so that that vast body of people, the sons of the labouring classes and the toilers, can get some kind of a reasonable education in the various trades and crafts. Everything has been said, I think, that' can be said upon this matter.
I would like to refer simply to this fact that we all know that unemployment is one of the pressing and most distressing matters that the governments, not only of this country, but of European countries, have to deal with. Happily the unemployment question is not a very prominent one in Canada at the present time, but the time has been when the question of unemployment was a serious matter and that time may come again. In the city of Berlin they have a clearing house for labour, known as the Berlin Labour Exchange, to which go those who are out of employment on the one hand and employers who want men on the other. It is an immense place where thousands of men assemble ^ every day and where hundreds are. placed in employment. At this clearing house it has been ascertained that very much the largest number of people who are seeking employment are unskilled labourers, that there is more unskilled labour seeking employment every day than there is labour in all the other trades combined. What does this prove? It proves that if men can get an education in some trade, business, or calling, they are not apt to be out of employment. The man who cannot get employment is the unskilled mechanic, while, if a man skilled in any line of business or in any trade does get out of employment, it is only as a rule temporary. The great body of men who are, practically, permanently out of employment are those belonging to the unskilled labour class. Surely that is a sufficient argument to prove to any government that it is the duty of the government to, as far as possible, educate the labouring classes in some trade or calling so that they may at all times have a trade upon which to rely and to fall back upon. If this commission were to issue I have no doubt whatever but that almost immediately upon its 1 Mr. MACDONELL.
being returned to this House and the report distributed throughout the country it would be made use of and be available in all parts of Canada. It would have a double use. It could be used for the purpose of giving information to the trades in different communities and provinces and it could be made the basis of further action by this government if the government sees fit to take this up, as it has taken up other matters of a kindred nature. As to the provincial aspect of this case, kindred subjects have already been dealt with by the government and therefore I do not anticipate any difficulty in dealing with it in such a way as not to violate the principle of provincial autonomy in regard to matters of education. It would not form a precedent for interference at any future time by this government with the matter of education. I think the resolution has been ably presented to this House. The difficulty of dealing with a question of education, which is entirely of provincial character, has been fully met by the arguments which have been presented and a few of which I have endeavoured to elucidate in the remarks which I have addressed to the House.

Mr. Speaker, the question which is now before the House interests me to a large degree, and it is especially interesting to those whom I represent. I strongly favour the resolution that has been presented by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). As has been truly said a change has taken place m the apprenticeship system. Now, it appears that they are anxious to produce a mechanic in three, four or five months instead of making him serve three or four years as they did in the past. I am not at this moment disposed to discuss the reasons which have brought about this change of affairs in the apprenticeship system, but I may state that this is one question and probably the only one in regard to which organized labour and the Manufacturers' Association agree. It is a very important question. My hon. friend who presented this resolution, as well as my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith), spoke about manual training. It was stated that organized labour is against manual training. In the real sense of the word organized labour is not against manual training, but it is against the taking of a clerk in a store, for instance, or anybody else, putting him into a training school for three months and trying to make a mechanic out of him. We claim, and I think justly, that it is impossible to teach a man how to do the work of a mechanic in three months. That has been the case in many trades. In the United States there are schools which advertise that if an employer wants a man of a certain trade they will produce him in three or four months. I might mention the Coyne

school in the plumbing trade which is carried on in New York and which follows this practice to a large extent. I am not disposed to sav in the House why this is done. The labour people are not against manual training. We have that ourselves in the city of Montreal. In my own trade, for instance, regular training is provided. We have two nights every week when young men can come and receive instruction in addition to the practical training which they get while working during the day. We want men in the trade, but we do not want to spoil our trade any more than a lawyer wants to spoil his profession. A trade is a profession after all. As far as I am concerned I see very little difference between a trade and a profession. Just as long as we have no law to protect ourselves, as long as we cannot come before this House or the provincial legislature and have our rules and regulations sanctioned, we have, to a large extent, to protect our profession. I want to go on record as saying right here, that labour is not against manual training provided it is done in the proper way. I am strongly in favour of and I hope the government will see its way clear to furnish sufficient money to train the labouring .classes of this country in the higher walks of artisanship. It is a great pity that today Canada has to send to different countries in the world for men to occupy the highest positions, and that Canadians should have to be satisfied to work under them. We Canadians have as much intelligence and as much energy as the people of any country in the world, and if facilities were afforded to the labouring classes to develop their natural ability I have not the slightest doubt that you would see the very best men springing from the ranks of the , people who labour.

Mr. Speaker; it is refreshing to know that occasionally a question may be brought before this House which can be considered from the national standpoint of what is best for Canada, and regardless altogether of party bias. I am glad that such a one is the question we have for consideration this evening. Any question that deals with the education of the masses of the people is important, and that the question now before us is important we are all agreed, as we also agree that it has been presented in a most able manner by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who moved the resolution. That hon. gentleman has submitted to us a verv practical question and he has asked that it be dealt with in a particular way. I venture to express the hope that the government may be willing to accede to the proposition set forth in the resolution, since, under the British North America Act, the provinces have bad relegated to them the work of providing systems of education. I am glad that learned gentlemen of the legal profession in this House are able to assure us tnat no strain will be placed upon the constitution should the resolution before us be adopted. For my own part I have always felt, and as the years go by I feel it more and more, that we have not in the truest sense of the term a national system of education in Canada. Since we cannot have that I am rejoiced to know that we will not be held to be trenching on the prerogative of the provinces should we adopt the scheme outlined in the resolution of my hon. friend. I trust, Sir, that the day may yet come when we will have a technical or trade school in every town of the land, and that the system will reach its apex in a national university established in the capital city of the Dominion. The resolution before us simply asks that an inquiry be instituted as to the merits of the proposition therein set forth. We ought not be unwilling to investigate; we ought not be unwilling to obtain from any and every quarter information which may tend towards the advancement of our people. I have no doubt that the commission which under this resolution would be appointed will view the question from a Canadian point of view, that they will see with Canadian eyes, hear with Canadian ears, and report back to us what is best in the older countries to suit our conditions and environment. It is something to have it recognized that there is such a thing as a Canadian point of view. To-day, I see that idea very fittingly given effect to by the Toronto 'Globe which is sending one of the best known newspaper men of Canada, Mr. Stewari Lyon, to report back to the Canadian people the conditions under which the political battle is being waged in England so that Canadians will not have the news filtered through American or even British sources, but through a Canadian channel and from the viewpoint of the Canadian people. Now, these centres of the old world. Germany, England, Belgium, and other continental countries in which for a long time they have had trade schools in operation will be visited by Canadian representatives and we shall have described from the Canadian point of view the adaptability of these various systems of education to the Dominion of Canada. That ought to be of considerable value to us. I was glad indeed to hear the mover of the resolution express himself as willing that the scope of this inquiry should be enlarged. The resolution speaks of an inquiry onlv into the matter of technical education, and my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) has stated his willingness to include an inquiry into manual training and trade schools; a fact which I hope the govern ment will note in connection with the proposed appointment of the commission. In Blisses' encyclopedia of social reform pub-

lished in 1908 there is given a modem definition of technical education and manual training, and if you bear with me I will read that definition because it appears to me that it may be helpful to a clarifying of views held on this question outside this House even though those within its precincts may be already thoroughly informed on the subject I read:
Technical education and manual training: We include under this general heading three subjects which are distinct, although continually confounded in the public mind-trade education, technical education, and manual training. We consider them under one head, in order that, by placing the subjects side by side, the important differences between them may be clearly brought out. We commence with definitions. Trade education is the preparing of craftsmen for practical work in a particular trade. Technical education is the teaching of the sciences in their particular application to the material interests of man. A good trade-school may be a very poor technical school, while a good technical school is not of necessity a good trade-school. Manual training is different from either; it is instruction in the use of tools as a part of a complete educational discipline. Trade-schools seek to turn out craftsmen; technical schools seek to turn out scientific specialists and professional men, such as civil engineers, architects, &e.; manual training seeks to develop complete manhood and womanhood by developing dexterity of hand as well as head.
I trust that definition will be borne in mind should the government conclude to accede to the wishes of the mover of the resolution. A very charming and interesting contribution has been made to the debate by those gentlemen who may in the proper sense be held to be representatives of labour in this House. I was glad to hear the hon. gentleman from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) and the hon. gentleman from Mai-sonneuve (Mr. Verville) express their acquiescence in the suggestion that labour has no objection whatever to manual ^training in the proper acceptation of the term, being introduced into our schools. The knowledge that men have is of course only of value as it expresses itself in action, and the proposition is that the industrial classes of Canada may be as well equipped for their particular callings in life, for the duties and responsibilities of citizenship, by reason of the schooling placed at their disposal, as are those who are able to participate in the higher branches of learning and in the higher walks of life; and surely one of the duties of a representative institution in a democratic country like this should he to provide to the utmost facilities for the advancement and betterment of all sections of society which together make up the commonwealth of this great Dominion. I am well aware that outside of this House there are those who are altogether opposed to the proposition contained in the resolution before the House. There are Mr. FOWKE.
those who think that the educational system should continue as it is, devoting itself entirely to the classics, and that no man should be held to be educated unless he takes a classical course at one of our universities. The time was when two or three learned professions were very much looked up to and admired and were thought to be the sine qua non of everything proper in human society. I do not say that that day is past or will ever be past. I am bound to say, however, that useful as the physician may be in society, we prefer the prophylactics of common sense; we prefer to keep well rather,than to apply ourselves to any system of therapeutics whose only purpose is to make us well after we become sick. With regard to the lawyer, I suppose we may be asked to acquiesce in the suggestion that without him truth would perish fr.om off the face of the earth. I do not deny the proposition. The lawyer has his place in society, but we are glad to give him as wide a berth as possible. The clergyman, another member of the learned professions, has an important place. I see that the hon. member for Victoria and Hali-burton (Mr. Hughes) is not present this evening to pay his compliments to the clergy. We are perhaps all in the frame of mind to believe that a little teaching of the doctrine of total depravity would not be amiss-like the old lady wno wanted to join a certain church and was told that she would have to pass an examination by a board of elders and answer certain questions. 'What questions?' she asked. 'For instance, do you believe in total depravity? ' ' That's easy,' said she; ' I not only believe in it, but hope to practise it too.' So we do not hope to get along without the learned professions. I am glad that gentlemen of the learned professions this afternoon have emphasized the fact that the classical is not the only method by which men may be educated in order that they may make the best of themselves in life, and may attain to positions of importance in the industrial life of Canada and of the world.
The fact has been adverted to that we are already doing a good deal in aid of technical education. The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) a few moments ago pointed out that the great agricultural industry in Canada b*s been mar. vellously helped by what is really a course of technical education given on the experimental farms of this Dominion and' in the laboratories of those farms. This is an age of the chemist in agriculture as well as in other departments of life, and I have no doubt that millions of dollars have been added to the wealth of this Dominion by reason of the technical education which the farmers have been able to avail themselves of through the reports issued by the Dominion government in relation to their par-

ticular calling, and I hope that this work will go on and increase. But I am also glad to reflect that this country long ago came to believe that it could never attain to greatness as a nation by remaining a pastoral people. So we have entered the field of industrialism, and this has grown in all the provinces of the Dominion until it is estimated that we have to-day invested in industrial pursuits $850,000,000, having an output of $750,000,000 per annum, with perhaps one fourth of our total population dependent upon those pursuits. Yet we are only in our infancy as an industrial community, and we could not do a wiser thing than avail ourselves of the knowledge, the wisdom, the experience, of the countries of the old world which have brought industrialism to a high state of perfection, and with whom we have to compete if we send our products into the marts of the world. Another reason for the appointment of a commission arises from the fact that this is a country of untold wealth in natural products. Some of these have been referred to this afternoon, and speakers have dwelt upon the importance of our training men to be experts in particular departments of industrialism, so that we may, with Canadian capital and Canadian labour, avail ourselves to the full of those natural advantages which Providence has placed at our disposal. Some natural produces of great importance I could mention that have not been named this afternoon. This is a country of fur-bearing animals. Canada exports millions of dollars' worth of furs every year, and why? Simply because in the old world, by reason of technical education, men have learned to treat those furs in such a way as to make them the desire of all who may be able to purchase them. Why may we not hope to teach and train men on our own soil so that they will be able to treat those furs which are now sent to Leipsic and London to be returned here in a finished state? In the same way the long lustre wools of Canada are being sent to the United States under a tariff of ten cents a pound, netting to our farmers only about ten cents a pound, whereas if we had skill and machinery to apply to the raw product, we could have the same market and the same profits as now go to the manufacturers of the eastern states. To stop the export of these raw materials and to enable our people to work them up into finished articles by the use of Canadian capital and Canadian labour on Canadian soil is surely worthy the attention of Canadian legislators. In this new era upon which we are entering, this business era, this era of trade and commerce and manufacture, it 34
ought to come as an inspiring thought to us that the opportunity is presented now to place ourselves on record as true to the belief within us and to take such action that the men of this generation, the youth coming on the stage of activity, the boys and girls in our schools who are destined to enter upon the industrial life, may have every opportunity and privilege to make the best of themselves, each in his particular calling, that, any boy or girl anywhere under the sun is known to possess at this hour.
At the risk of wearying the House, I would like to tell you of some concrete instances myself, which prove the advantage of having out own experts in the manufacturing interests. I come from a town which has had a varied experience in industrial life. We have had corporations formed to carry on industries in that community, without the advantage of technical knowledge in relation to their undertaking. They had plenty of capital, the world was all before them, and yet they came to naught. To-day, however, we have a number of flourishing industries in that town-the town of Oshawa-which may be called the Manchester of Canada. One of these industries is the largest of its kind within the boundaries of the British empire; another is the largest of its kind in the Dominion. Both are what they really are today-one employing nearly a thousand men, and its capacity circumscribed only by its ability to get men, and it could enlarge its plant at any time if labour were at hand-both these industries owe their success, not to their abundance of capital, but to the expert knowledge and training of the men in charge. One of these establishments started as a blacksmith shop on the side of the road, but the owner was a skilled mechanic, and under his management that has grown to be the largest institution of the kind in the empire to-day Why? Simply because the man at its head has skill and knowledge and is an expert in his particular line. The other industry I refer to owes its growth to the very same reason. One of its proprietors, and one of the finest inventors in the Dominion, is the manager of that business, and the president of the company told me only a few days ago that because of the skill of that particular man, of whom he is very proud, he is able to-day to start three new industries of a kind not now being operated anywhere in Canada, and will do so as soon as the right sort of men to manage them are available. So that there is any amount of scoper for an educational institution such as we have in our mind to-night.
It has been shown by the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution (Mr. Guth-lie) that there is a current of public opin-

1C59

ion all over the country behind this movement. It is endorsed by the trade and labour councils and by the boards of trade and chambers of commerce, and the public sentiment in every manufacturing town and mercantile community is entirely favourable to the proposition. I therefore sincerely hope,-in view of all the circumstances, that the government will not be frightened away from the adoption of the idea by any regard for the small cost which the appointment of a commission would entail, and I hope they will not be alarmed by the bogey that it would place a strain on the constitution greater than it could bear. I trust that the House and government will give their favourable consideration to this most important resolution, so ably presented by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) this afternoon.

I do not rise for the purpose of making any extensive remarks upon the resolution before the House, but for the purpose of tendering my sincere thanks to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) for having introduced this resolution. I am sure that any hon. gentleman who heard him present this matter before the House must have come to the conclusion that there is nothing to prevent the government coming to the assistance of industrial training. Coming from the province of Nova Scotia, where we have already a splendid technical school, established lately in the city of Halifax by the local government, and also a manual training school, second to none in the Dominion, of which we are very proud, I might be *content with that condition and give no heed to the rest of Canada. But that is not the way we are built down there. We are always glad to help the rest of Canada, even though sometimes, when we -seek a little consideration for our province, the rest of Canada looks at us with rather a forbidding eye. However, should this government come to the conclusion to assist technical education throughout Canada- while I am not in the position to speak for the government of Nova Scotia-yet I am sure I can say that the government of that province will be very glad indeed to accept any assistance for the carrying on of that school, without feeling that such a grant would interfere with their provincial rights m any way.
Ship building has been referred to by the mover of this resolution. One of the good reasons for instituting a technical school in Nova Scotia is that we expect to have a ship building plant there very shortly and we hope-because our people are very apt and quick to learn-to have men comnetent to take charge of the principal positions in connection with that in-Mr. FOWKE.
dustry. Navigation has also been referred to. I am sorry to say that in the maritime provinces we have no navigation school, and if there be any school this government should establish, it ought to be a school of navigation. Trade and navigation go hand in hand, and this government would be doing a great deal for trade and commerce and navigation by giving its assistance to the establishment of a school of navigation- It is a great disadvantage to the maritime provinces not to have a school. Several men competent to teach that branch have taken it up but could not carry it on because, although at times they had sufficient pupils, at other times they had not. Therefore it would be a good thing for this government to take that question into consideration. While I think that the government should contribute to all branches of industrial training, certainly I think it should contribute to the teaching of navigation, some contribution should be made towards the teaching of that subject in our technical school in Nova Scotia. We have been accustomed, particularly in the eastern mining sections of Canada, to go across the border for our mining engineers, but the government of Nova Scotia have now established mining schools which have done a great deal for us in providing and preparing men to act as mining engineers. Some of the industries which have been established fn Nova Scotia almost went to destruction shortly after their inception. When the sugar refinery was established in Halifax technical men were brought from the United States to conduct it. The result was that it looks suspiciously as if these men did not attempt to carry on the industry properly and in a very few years the industry had gone altogether and the capital invested in it was practically sunk. After getting a fresh start and depending more on the men who had gained a little information in regard to the manufacture of sugar in our own province, that industry has become a great success. If we had had technical education it would have been of great assistance to us in the establishment of that industry as well as in connection with our cotton factory and many other industries.
While I should be glad to see this resolution passed, I do not think that the appointment of a commission is necessary. I do not believe that a commission could obtain any more information, any better.collection of facts and could place them before this House in better order than has been done by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) this afternoon. The commission is not necessary. This matter should be taken up by the government at once, and they could easily see the advantage from every standpoint of taking action in this direction. As has

been well stated here, there are many industries in the Dominion of Canada that have barely been touched upon yet. Take, for instance, the pulp wood industry. Great quantities of pulp as well as many other products of Canada are shipped to the United States in the raw state. If we had technical education, if our people were prepared to take hold of the different industries, such as the pulp wood industry and in place of sending abroad partly manufactured products to be returned to us m the finished state, should send out finished products, it would be greatly to the benefit of Canadian manufactures and of Canada generally. I believe that if the government would take action on the statement of facts as presented by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) the country would endorse them in providing at least 25 to 30 per cent of the cost of taking care of any technical school that maybe started in any province. The hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) stated that in the German empire they pay 28 per cent, and I think that this government would be perfectly justified in arranging to contribute to the extent of 25 to 30 per cent of the -cost of running any technical school in any province in the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I am only voicing the opinion of every member of this House when I say that our "thanks are due to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) for having brought this important subject to the attention of parliament and for the exceptionally able, forceful and comprehensive manner in which he introduced his resolution. I think, too, Sir, the House is to be congratulated on the very full discussion which has taken place on this resolution, to be congratulated because the subject is one which, no matter what view we may take as to the jurisdiction of this government or a provincial government to deal with it, cannot be viewed other than as one of great national concern. I should like to add a fbw words to what has already been said from that point of view, but before doing so I would like to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. R. Smith) in, reference to industrial accidents in the coal mines of Nova Scotia and the coal mines of British Columbia.
The hon. member has drawn the attention of the House to the great difference in the number of accidents which have taken place in the mines of those two provinces, and I do not know that a more fortunate example could-have been brought forth to illustrate the important part which technical education may play in the industrial development of a nation than the example the hon. gentleman has cited. During recess I took advantage of 34i
the oportunity to look up a table showing the number of fatal and serious -accidents in the coal mines of Nova Scotia and British Columbia, and I find that in the last ten years in Nova Scotia 264 miners have been killed outright in the course of their employment, while in the province of British Columbia, 624 miners have been killed outright in the course of their employment. Reducing the figures to averages, the difference is still more striking. Taking the rate per thousand men employed in Nova Scotia and comparing it with the ratio per thousand men employed m the mines of British Columbia, we find that the fatal accidents in Nova Scotia have been 2-64 per thousand men employed and in British Columbia, 9 ;21. That, Sir, is to be accounted for, it seems to me, mostly by the different advantages given to the miners of those two provinces in the way of technical education. My hon. friend knows, as every member of this House knows, that factory legislation and legislation in regard to mines is enacted by the provincial legislatures. He knows that the mining inspectors, as the factory inspectors, are appointed by the governments of the respective provinces, and I believe that from the point of view of laws -and numbers of inspectors, the conditions in British Columbia will compare favourably with those in Nova Scotia. But there is this difference between the two provinces: In the province of Nova Scotia you have to-day a Department of Technical Education and since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, you have had technical schools in connection with the mines of that province so that when the miners who are spending their day time in the mine have an evening or have leisure, they may get the advantages of a technical training which will help to acquaint them with the difficulties and the hazardous conditions of their calling, with the scientific side of the work in which they are engaged. The result of that is shown in the figures that have been placed before the House. It seems to me the hon. gentleman has rendered to this country a great service in drawing attention to the fact that technical education may be the means of saving to the nation a large part of its working population.
Let me supplement these figures in regard to mining by some figures which the Department of Labour has been gathering during the last few years in regard to the subject of industrial accidents generally. Although the figures are imperfect, -although they do not begin to include the total number of accidents which have taken place, they are, I think, sufficiently large to show how important this particular phase of industrial life is. Taking the figures as reported in the annual report of the Depart-

ment of Labour, for the vear ending March 31, 1909, I find that the number of person? engaged in industrial occupations who were killed outright from accidents occurring in the course of their work, was 1,271 and during the preceding year, the total number was 1,353. Take that average for a period of ten years, and what does it amount to? Between 13,000 and 14,000 of the wage earners, of the wealth producers of this country, killed outright in the course of their employment. What a tremendous national loss this is, to say nothing of the great loss to industry, to say nothing of what it means to the friends and families of those who are victims of these disasters. We see here the necessity for an extension of governmental action which may help to acquaint workingmen with the difficulties and dangers attendant on their callings, and which may tend in some'way to reduce the number of fatal accidents which are likely to occur.
Now, I would like to say a word or two on another phase of the importance of technical education. And first of all, let me draw attention to the important part which technical education must necessarily play in the industrial development of this or of anv other nation at the present time- must play because of the change which has taken place in the methods under which industrv is carried on to-day in comparison with the methods under which it was carried on in the past. Under the old system as it prevailed before the mechanical inventions that have taken place during the last century, under the old domestic system, it was the custom of the employer to work with his men in his own home or in the shop. There were not then the large factories^ there were not the large organizations of capital and of labour .as we find them to-day. Under the old system of industrv the training of the artisan was a comparatively simple matter, but under the system as it has developed today through the introduction of different powers the harnessing of the forces of nature, be they water, steam or electricity, we have entered into an entirely different industrial era, we have an industrial condition in which technical education must play a tremendous part. No man, for instance, can deal with electricity unless he is something more than an ordinarv workingman, something more than an ordinary mechanic; he must have scientific training if he is to take any part in the application of electrical power to industry. Our whole industrial system being carried on to-day by factory organization and organization of capital and labour on a large scale, renders it abso-lutelv essential that a nation which is going to progress and keep abreast of the times must eauio its workers along the most modern lines, provide its workers Mr. KING.
with a practical technical training to enable them to deal with the new conditions under which they are obliged to work.
But not onlv has the industrial system vastly changed from what it was some years ago, the nature of the competition in industry has become vastly different from what it was not so long ago. It is no longer in any line of manufacture a question of competition as between municipality and municipality, as between nrovince and province, but it is a world wide competition, competition between one nation and another, between different countries forming a part of the same empire, and between different empires, a struggle for industrial supremacy so vast that it is difficult for the imagination to grasp its significance. Now, in a struggle such as that carried on under our industrial system, the slightest difference in processes, in technical devices, the slightest advantage in scientific knowledge, in the adaptability of machinery for different purposes, may have a far reaching effect. It may affect the whole of one industry, or the industries of one country, as compared with those of another country, and we in Canada, who at this time are endeavouring, as we all are, to become one of the foremost peoples in the industrial struggle of our time, should be prepared to consider carefully this question of technical education, since upon technical education will largely depend the success of our manufacturers in obtaining the advantage of the latest scientific processes. Not only the men who are directing an industry, but also those who are taking part in it, must be well educated to enable our country to hold its own and make headway against all competitors.
Sir, while speaking on this question of foreign competition, I would like to touch for a moment on the question of foreign trade. No nation that is worthy the name can hope to accomplish much unless it develops a large foreign trade, and this country, while it has already made considerable strides in the direction of gaining a foothold in the markets of Europe and elsewhere, will, we hope, go much further, and not only maintain a foothold in the markets of Europe, but also gain an entrance in the markets of the Orient, for which we are so well fitted by our geographical position. Perhaps the House will pardon me if I make a reference to one or two facts which came under my observation during the time I was privileged to be in the Orient last year. What impressed me almost more than anything else was the extent to-which the manufacturers of England, the manufacturers of Germany and the manufacturers of the United States were finding a sale for their goods in those distant parts. In the cities of China, in the towns and cities of Japan, one saw

everywhere articles of manufacture, products of one kind or another, coming from Great Britain, from Germany and other countries of Europe, and also from the United States; and I could not but wonder as a Canadian that we had not found our wav into those distant parts, possessing, as 1 have mentioned, a great natural geo-granhical advantage in the matter of trade with the far east. Going down from China to Japan, one travels through Manchuria on a road over rails that are made in Europe, and on cars that are made in the United States. The table service is made up of cutlery and china ,hat comes from Great Britain. Much of the food has been prepared in European countries or in the United States. Surely we can hope that before long the manufacturers and producers of this country will be finding a market for their goods in those distant regions, and this market, I believe, once it is obtained, will be one of the iaigest and most profitable in the world. But if we are to find an entrance to that market, and if we are to hold our own when we get there, it will be only in virtue of the fact that our industries are equipped in a manner second to none as compared with those of other countries, and that we are doing a business as up-to-date as that which any other nation can do.
But, if there was one thing that impressed me more than another it was the extraordinary industrial development which has taken place in those countries themselves, and that is one of the main reasons why we should spare neither time nor money in an endeavour to equip our industrial communities in the most efficient manner if we are going, not only to obtain a foothold in those foreign countries, but if at the same time we are to retain our own markets in face of the competition which is sure to come from the far east. Let me mention only one case. I had the privilege of visiting the city of Hankow, which is three days' journey up the Yangtsze river, just opposite on the other side of the river, is located a large iron and steel industry. At the time I was there, this concern, established by Chinese capital, employed in the vicinity of 20,000 Chinese workmen, and they were shipping pig iron and steel ingots not onlv to other cities of China but to the United States as well, paying the duty on the steel ingots all that distance from the interior of China, across the Pacific, paying the duty and landing that steel at a profit in the very districts in which steel is being manufactured in the United States. I asked myself how it was p'ossibie that the Chinese nation that we had supposed to be asleep was carrying on so successfully such an industry in the far east, and the answer
I found in connection with the very subject we are considering to-night. The men who were directing those industries were highly trained specialists, some of these young Chinese who had^gone to Germany, who had gone to the United States, who had gone to Great Britain to receive a technical education in the schools and colleges there, and with that fine intellectuality characteristic of Chinamen, were able to return to their own country and to take part in an industrial development which will be second to none in the near future.
Now, if we are going to hold our own against that kind of competition it will only be by bringing our workmen up to the highest degree of efficiency, and by seeing that our industries are managed by men who are second to none in technical knowledge and training. They talk of the Yellow peril. Sir, I nnd no danger in the Yellow peril if you consider it under the aspect of immigration. I believe that can be dealt with by diplomacy; I believe it will be possible to keep the oriental to his own side of the Pacific, as it is in every way desirable he should bo kept. The real Yellow peril, a peril tha1 is surely coming, is that of industrial competition with the Orient, and when it does come in all its power, it will present to us the greatest problem with which this continent has yet been faced. Let me show wherein it is at our doors at this very moment. I have in my pocket a letter I received from a gentleman in San Francisco, v. ho says that the company with which he is concerned is to-day in a position to control the imports of steel billets, from the company in China to which I have referred, and his company is arranging with that company in Hankow to secure their products, the steel billets and pig iron they are manufacturing tnere, and he writes to know what are the possibilities of his developing with this material a large iron and steel industry and_rolling mills on our Pacific coast. His company is proposing to establish a manufacturing concern somewhere on the western slope of the United States and Canada to carry on the manufacture of steel with their products coming from this old country of China. Now what is true there is going to be true in one industry after another, and how are we to meet it? It will not be met by our shorter hours of labour.	We work eight to ten
hours a day in our factories, whereas the orientals are working twenty-four hours in the concern to which I have referred, thev never stop even for Sundays, the Chinese New Year being the only day in which that industry closes down. Our regard for women in industry is not going to save us, our laws exempting little children from working in these industries is not going to

save us. Our higher wages will not the better enable us to meet this competition. What then is going to save us? Two things, and two things alone will enable this country to face the competition with which it is destined to be brought into conflict in the far east. One of these is the extent which the future witnesses the spreading of the light of the new world over the old, spreading of the light from the lamp of knowledge, and the still brighter radiance of Christian truth and Christian influence. Where that goes 'will come with it a greater regard and respect for women, a greater reverence for the little child, a greater and truer insight into the nature and dignity of manhood itself. With these things will come a shortening in the hours of labour, a lessening of the employment of women and children, and a respect for the Sunday which we observe as a day of rest, and a hundred and one other considerations which makes this our standard of living what it is among our own people. The other thing that mav help us to meet this competition is the greatness of our natural resources, combined with the industrial efficiency of our own working people, and this industrial efficiency can only be brought about by the development on a general scale throughout the whole Dominion of sound technical education, carried on by the authorities whose duty it is to do it. Only by the development of this system of technical education so far as we can possibly carry it, will we be in a position to face the future with a confidence of success.
Now, Sir, perhaps I have spoken on this point at greater length than the circumstances would warrant. But I have thought that perhaps another opportunity may not occur very soon to enable me to express my views on a question which seems to me of paramount importance. It seems to me there is great need for the development of a system of technical education in Canada. This need has been demonstrated in half a dozen different ways. First of all, it has been demonstrated by comparison of conditions in this country with conditions as they are in Germany, in France, in England, in Switzerland and in the United States. It has been shown by the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution and by others who have spoken on it, how much has been done by each of these countries in the- matter of promoting technical education. The hon. leader of the opposition asked, I think, in speaking of Germany, whether the work that has been carried on there had been done for the most part by the states. I think the work has been carried on by the states in Germany, for the most part. The work was started in Germany, as the member for South Wellington said this afternoon, away back early in the last century, and it has been taken up by Mr. KING.
one state after another. But the federal government in Germany has also done something to further this work. They have done nothing in the way of teaching, but they have established an institute for physical and technical research, they have an industrial museum, and they are giving financial assistance to ship-building and navigation schools. In the United States while most of the work has been carried on by the individual states, the federal government contributed land away back in 1862 for the purpose of aiding in the development of the agricultural and mechanical arts. They have had one or two commissions which have made inquiries into these questions, and a department of education which conducts researches along these lines. The federal government has also granted financial aid to the several states. In Great Britain there have been a large number of polytechnic schools, continuation classes, and technical schools and commercial and technical universities. All these countries are competitors of Canada, and are doing a great deal to equip their army of workers and enable them to take their part in this world wide competition. And were there no other reason why the authorities of this country should do their part in promoting the work of technical education than that our competitors are doing so that of itself would be a strong reason [DOT]vhy much should be done. But there is another reason that was mentioned by the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) and the hon. member for Guysboro (Mr. Sinclair), and that is that the employers of labour in this country are crying out for skilled workmen. We all know that .this demand comes from every part of the Dominion, one industry after another complaining that they have not enongh skill'd workmen. They allege that they have to send to other countries to get foremen, and import men skilled in certain industries. Why is this ? It is :iot because we have not in Canada men who are capable of becoming skilled in scientific knowledge, and of carrying on any industry after the most modern" scientific methods, but it is because we have not in Canada a sufficient number of institutes to enable our artisans and workingmen to qualify for these high positions the number of which is daily increasing. Not only is there a desire on the part of the employers for a greater number of skilled workmen but there is also, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve, the mover of the resolution and the hon. member for Nanaimo have said, a desire on the part of the workingmen themselves to avail themselves of greater opportunities, of education in this direction. I think it was the hon. member for South Wellington who pointed out that not less than three-quarters of a million of dollars was spent by the work-

men of this country in payments to the correspondence schools in the United States in the furthering of this work of selfeducation along technical lines. Where there is a desire to that extent, manifesting itself in that particular way, surely we have before us the strongest reason why the authorities, whose duty it may be to undertake this work, should undertake it to the greatest degree possible.
And, Sir, there is another reason, much akin to the one which I have already mentioned, and that is the need at this time for a better system of apprenticeship. Our industries are suffering in everv direction because workingmen do not go through the form of apprenticeship now that they went through in the olden days. It is inevitable that it should be so. In the olden days the apprentice worked with his employer in his master's shop, but to-day the employer is a large corporation and this personal relationship which formerly existed is now impossible. There is the greatest diversity of industry, and the greatest division of labour, so that the work of the ordinary mechanic comes often to be that of simply performing one particular kind of action, doing that in a monotonous, routine fashion and knowing nothing of the whole process of which his labour forms a part. That beiir" so it seems to me there is a greater need for some system of education which will make intelligible to the man who has the work to do the part which he is performing in industrial development and that service might be performed by an extension of the system of technical education throughout the country.	_
There is a further feature which I think should be considered in this connection and it is the obligation which society owes to workingmen to enable them to realize the best of the capacity which they have within them. This is something which we, in this day, are too apt to forget. We have all the comforts in our homes, we think of the enjoyments that we possess of one kind and another, but we fail to realize to what a considerable extent, I was going to say, the almost illimitable extent, the whole enjoyment and routine of our daily life rests upon the manner in which the great mass of men who are day labourers or ordinary mechanics discharge the duties which they are called unon to perform. Let me read an extract from the report of the Industrial Committee of the American Federation of Labour which recently held its session in the city of Toronto. It was a report brought in by a committee of the workingmen composing that body in regard to this question of industrial education and the sentence or two which I shall read is deserving of the consideration not only of this House but of every man in this country:
We must never lose sight of the fact that a large majority of the working people are poor, and because of this they are forced to begin the battle of life at an early age. The need of the day is that something be done for the children of this great wage-working class.
Formerly the apprentice system offered the boy an opportunity to learn a trade and become a thoroughly trained mechanic, but of late years the scheme of specialization has supplanted the old apprenticeship system, even to extreme specialization. It ought to be recognized as a scientific truth that the higher the skill possessed by the mechanic the more valuable his labour, both to himself, his employer and the community.
The one trouble in America to-day is that too many of our youths who have graduated from the grammar or high schools are misfits industrially. If we are to secure industrial supremacy, or even maintain our present standards in the industrial world, we must in some way in our educational system acquire an equivalent to our old apprenticeship system.
It is to the first paragraph of that extract that I would like t.o direct special attention.
A large majority of the working people are poor, and because of this they are forced to begin the battle of life at an early age. The need of the day is that something be done tor the children of this great wage-working class.
We leave these halls of parliament, we go to our homes in the evening, we take a street car, we so to our rooms and sit down by our firesides and unless there is a strike on the street railway, or a strike of plumbers so that our houses are cold when we go into them, unless there is a strike of miners so that we cannot get coal for our fires, or unless there is some other kind of industrial disturbance to direct our attention to the fact that there is a great industrial community working ceaselessly day and night, we are all too apt to forget that this great body of workers exists at all. For that reason we cannot too often remind ourselves of the fact that society does owe something to the great body of working people who are obliged to begin life early, to begin to toil before their education is completed, that we owe something to them in the way of conferring an opportunity at least to each to realize the capacities of which his nature may be capable. Carlyle says, in one of his famous works, that for a man to die ignorant who has capacity for knowledge, is a tragedy. Well, Sir, if this be true, the crime must somewhere rest upon the heads of those who have it within their power to confer the opportunity and who yet withhold it. It seems to me therefore that if we recognize the imperative ethical obligation which is upon us we will find it out dutv to do something to put in the way of the miner who daily risks his life in underground toil the opportunty for education which will better enable him to rise in the calling
