While I have endeavoured to lay emphasis on the need for the extension of the work I would have failed to have properly presented to the House what I had in my mind had I conveyed the impression that Canada is not at the present time doing a great deal considering the number of other things that we have been called upon to do and the comparatively early stage of our industrial development. Just running over in a very rapid way what has been accomplished, let me direct the attention of the House to the province of Nova

Scotia. They have in that province a department of technical education. In that respect the province of Nova Scotia, as in some other respects, has gone far and away ahead of any of the other provinces of the Dominion. They have recognized the great importance of this work to the extent of having a department of the government under an able and efficient officer, Dr. Sexton, devoting its time exclusively to the work of technical education.
Thev have, I understand, 21 technical schools established in different districts throughout the province and these schools are attended by miners, by stationary engineers, by fishermen, and by craftsmen generally. It is, I believe, the intention of the provincial government to still further extend that work which was initiated by the Hon. Mr. Fielding, when he was premier of Nova Scotia. In Prince Edward Island something is being done in the way of manual training and in New Brunswick there is a department of forestry connected with the university, but little has been undertaken in the way of technical education in either of these provinces. In the province of Quebec a good deal has already been done and more is promised. Recently, Sir Lomer Gouin, the premier, in connection with the laying of the foundation stone of a new technical institute in Montreal promised that the government recognizing the needs of the mechanics and working classes, would make for still further progress in this line. There are at present 11 schools of arts and manufactures in the province of '*nh'-'c: there have been liberal grants to existing institutions and the premier has promised to the city of Quebec a technical institute similar to that in course of construction in Montreal. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, experiencing the need for skilled mechanics, has started in connection with the Angus shops, classes for the technical education of its employees, and the classes, I am informed, are well attended. The universities of McGill and Laval have done good work in their technical branches, so that the province of Quebec has set to the other provinces of the Dominion an example which is only paralleled by Nova Scotia and Ontario. In Ontario, the development of technical education and manual training through the high schools and collegiate institutes has gone a long way, and there are also well equipped technical high schools at Hamilton and Toronto. The university has its school of Practical Science and department of forestry, there is the agricultural school at Guelph, and the department of mines at Kingston. Within the last few months the technical high schools at Toronto sent a commissioner to the United States to inquire into the conditions there, and the pro-

vincial government has sent another commissioner to Europe to inquire into technical education, so that it may be said that Ontario is doing good work in this direction. The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) has spoken of what is being done in his own province and in his own city, and I would like to mention the commendable example set by the late David A. Mitchell, of Winnipeg, who, in his will, provided a large sum to be devoted to the erection of technical schools in which workingmen and artisans may receive free of charge technical training.at evening classes in their particular callings. This probably sums up all that has been done throughout the Dominion in the way of technical education. It is only a few years since the start was made, but what has been done thus far gives us reason to hope that these provinces will advance in the work and that their example will be followed by the other provinces.
The resolution before the House expresses the opinion that it is advisable that a committee of inquiry should be forthwith appointed to investigate the needs of Canada in this respect to technical education and to report the ways and means by which these needs may best be met. There can be no doubt that such a commission would render great service to the Dominion, and to all the provinces of the Dominion. The reports of the British consular agents afford very interesting information as to what is being done by other c^'mtries in the way of gathering information on the subject of technical education. I have here a list of British consular reports on technical education in Germany which I find in the library of the Department of Labour, and I will read it to show what information may be acquired by gentlemen who make researches into existing conditions in other countries. There is one report of 83 pages which deals with special schools and courses for mechanical engineering in Germany. There is another report of 91 pages dealing with what Germany has done for the development of the textile interests, another report on navigation schools, another report on the special technical schools for the ceramic industry, another report on agricultural instruction in Germany, another report on engineering schools, another report on the technical schools for the branches of the metal industry, another on technical instruction in naval construction and architecture, another on special schools for ship engineers, and another on special schools for the woodworking industry.
_ Now, if the great nation of Britain finds it to her commercial and industrial advantage to have her consular agents prepare reports on what a rival nation is doing to
develop industries along technical lines, that should be evidence enough to show wherein a similar course adopted by the governments that have charge of thi- particular work could be found advantageous to them, and that the work of any commission properly performed would be of great service to this country. 1 may say that the Department of Labour has already commenced to gather a large amount of information on this subject of technical education in other countries, and any work which a commission would undertake would be in part of that nature. So far as it has been possible to do it by means of correspondence we have endeavoured in the Department of Labour to gather in the library reports on what is being done for technical education in tin-different countries of the world. We shall be only too glad in the department to have any persons w'ho are interested in this subject take advantage of the information which is gathered there. Mr. Acland, the deputy minister, who has made a very full and careful study of this whole question would be pleased, I am sure, to lend his assistance towards facilitating the work of representatives of the provincial governments or others who may desire to consult any of the documents in the department.
There does not seem to be any diffe-ence of opinion as to the desire in many quarters for a commission of this kind. That has been made plain to us by the manufacturers as well as the workingmen through their representatives in the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Federation of Labour, each of which bodies have made requests that something should be done in this direction. It goes without saying that the recommendations on this subject from boards of trade, universities and other public bodies, are also entitled to the greatest respect and consideration. But that leads to a further point which has been mentioned this evening. All that I have said thus far has had relation to the importance ol technical education; and I think every member of the House will agree that there is little room for difference of opinion as to the importance of this matter to Canada as a young nation seeking industrial supremacy be it ever so far removed. We cannot, I think, overestimate the importance of this work, no matter by whom it may be carried on. Much has been said of Germany. I think the commercial and industrial historv of Germany is most enlightening to this country. It was after the downfall of Napoleon that Prussia saw her opportunity to become a great nation. She started in the work of nation-building by laying the foundations sure and strong, bv endeavouring to establish without delay systems of technical training which would make her working-

men and artisans second to no others on earth. Then, alter the Franco-German war, the large indemnity paid by Trance left the provinces free to expend on technical education what they wotnd otherwise not have been au,e to devote to that object. From the fact that the provinces themselves made the beginning at the time they did, and from this other exceptional advantage, Germany has been able, since the time of the birth of the empire, to take the strides that have brought her to the position of industrial importance she holds in the world a.t the present time; and I think Canada is a young country, looking forward to tile part she shall play, as the largest and most import-an part of the British empire, can afford to take lessons out of the books of any other nation in the world and profit by them.
But there is left the doubt _ on the question of jurisdiction, and that is a matter which cannot be too carefully considered I do not believe that too much importance can be attached to the work of technical education to be done by the authorities whose duty it is to perform that work. But it is another question whether or not this parliament has the power to go into this question to the extent to which some speakers this evening have indicated they would like to see it do. The resolution asks only for a commission to inquire into the needs of this country. It suggests, however, that the commission should also report on ways and means. Other speakers have suggested that the government should do more than that-that it should assist in a financial way; and other speakers, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) in particular, went so far as to express the wish that the word ' commission ' had been left out of the resolution altogether-though if it had been, I fail to see how there would have been any resolution left

and would prefer that the government should do something in a practical way. in the direction of instruction along technical lines. All of this raises a question which has been debated many times in this House, and one which we cannot consider too carefully-whether or not the good which might be done by the appointment of a body by this government to further the work of technical education might not be in part undone by the mischief which the appointment of such a body might create were the motives and purposes of this government in establishing such a commission not fully comprehended and understood. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has said that communications have already been received to the effect that there would be no objection on the part of the provinces to such a course. Well, Sir. it seems to me that before the Dominion government should take the step suggested in the resolution, there should be some-thins more than this negative attitude on . Mr. KING.
the part of the provinces. It should not be a case of no objection, but a case of an earnestly expressed desire which the government should be asked to listen to._ I think, the risk should not be run of raising a great constitutional question in a matter of such great national importance until at least the exact position of this government with regard to this question is fully and rightly understood by the different provinces and by the people in the country. To my mind the section of the British North America Act which says that ' the legislatures may exclusively make laws in relation to education, undoubtedly gives to the provinces the right of legislation in all matters respecting education; and if this parliament were to attempt to legislate on matters affecting education, as set forth in this section. I think this parliament would be going beyond the powers which are given to it in the British North : meric a Act. But I am not so sure that the exclusive right to make laws with regard to education means the right to exclude the Dominion from gathering information on any subject which may be deemed a subject of national importance. However, that may be a debatable constitutional question, and in view of the importance of the subject of this discussinon, I think it would be well if the mover of this resolution would_ allow the government a further opportunity to consider the question from this point of view, and not press it to a division to-night. Assuming that we got over the question of jurisdiction all right, there is still the question of the advisability and the expediency of taking this step so long as there is any likelihood of that step being misunderstood; and I hope that one of the results of this debate will be that the true relationship of the provinces to the Dominion on this question of great national concern will be brought out in bolder and clearer relief than ever before, and if the subject be brought up again, as I hope it will be, there will be no doubt in the mind of any member of this House, or in any group of responsible persons outside, as to whether or not the Dominion would he trespassing in endeavouring to co-operate with the provin-oes-for it is co-operation alone that would be expected-to the extent the mover of this resolution would desire. I would beg to move therefore the adjournment of the debate.

Before the debate is adjourned, I desire to congratulate the mover of this resolution, (Mr. Guthrie) and the various other gentlemen who have snoken and who have shown such a wide range of information, upon having brought this matter so forcibly and clearly to the attention of the country. In a comnaratively new and almost undeveloped country such as Canada, it would be seen to be eminently

wise, in the first place, to take stock, as it were, of the resources which the country possesses, and in the next place endeavour to come to a conclusion as to the most effective way by which those resources can be developed. The industrial development of Germany has been alluded to by more than one speaker to-day. When we consider the thoroughness with which the German empire has laid the foundations of its great industrial development, and when we realize how comparatively nothing has been done in this country along the same lines, we cannot but wonder that Canada has made so great an industral advance as she has attained to. Her progress in that respect speaks volumes for the ability, energy and aptiiuue of our neople. 1 do not desire to labour the question of how important it is that there should be industrial training and technical education in this country. We are all pretty much agreed with regard to that. Take the professional man, the lawyer, the clergyman, you find that each of them has the advantage of a special training after he has finished his academic course. To a certain extent a farmer also has the advantage of such a technical training or education. But, as has been well said by the mover of this resolution (Mr. Guthrie) and my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) and others, when we come to look at the great majority of the labouring population, we find that they remain, in this respect, under enormous disabilities, which ought to be removed at the earliest possible moment.
My hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) has made a very comprehensive speech. He has spoken very warmly on this point. He has spoken of the Yellow peril in the shape of industrial competition from the oriental countries, and this peril, he says, is not remote but it is at our door today. He has spoken of the disabilities of the working classes and the inability of our labouring population to utilize their time to the best advantage. He discussed many matters, and one would have thought that even so mild a resolution as that of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) would have seemed to the hon. minister but a lame and impotent conclusion. The Minister of Labour, however, is not prepared to go even that far, and he conjures up some imaginary constitutional objection. I listened to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) with a great deal of interest, and I think that as regards the constitutional question, he need not have laboured it to one-tenth the extent he did. He made an absolutely convincing case so far as that is concerned. If the position of the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) be correct, the government has been violating the constitution of Canada for 35 or 40 years in the establishment of the military school in Kingston. But I have not heard of any province
raising any objection. But the hon. minister need not stop at the Kingston military school, let him look at the estimates of this year or any year, and he will find over and over again, where the government has spent moTiev bv the million on matters absolutely within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. Does not my hon. friend know that his own estimates which he has just brought down, contain dozens of items for aid to undertakings purely local and absolutely within the jurisdiction of the local legislatures. Local works and undertakings, except in so far as they connect one province with another or some province with a country outside Canada, are purely and absolutely within provincial control, yet you can take the estimates and on page after page you will find money given by the $5,000, $10,000 and $100,000 to undertakings of that kind. The parliament of Canada has the right to vote money for any purpose that it may deem proper. It has voted money for purposes absolutely outside Canada. For example to aid the sufferers at San Francisco, to industrial exhibitions within our own country, subsidies to provincial railways which are purely works of a local character and under provincial jurisdiction, aid to arts schools, special lectures upon the advantages of the metric system, a grant to McGill university in aid of work" of this kind, schools for the examinations of masters and mates, to keep up the school at Kingston and for the establishment of experimental farms. When we have had illustrations. of the sort every year for the last 15 or 25 years in every set of estimates brought down, is it not absolutely perfect folly to talk about there being any constitutional objection whatever to granting aid immediately to technical education in this country. We can do it and no one can say us nay. If the Minister of Labour has no better answer to his own impressive speech than the one he gave at the end of it, I venture to think, he would do better to adhere to the first part of his speech, and not the last, and that the government should act in this matter at once. I would have thought that, after the information vouchsafed this afternoon, he would have said to my hon. friend from_ South Wellington:	Your motion is
well intended, you desire that a commission shall be appointed for the purpose of inquiring into the needs of Canada in respect of technical education, but we know the needs of Canada now, we know that this country is behind almost every country in the world in that respect, we have the example of Germany, we have the reports of the commissions in Germany, we have the example of the United States and the reports of the technical commissions in that country, we have the example of the British Islands and the reports of the technical commissions there, and consequently we have at least enough to know that some-

thing ought to be done and done quickly in this regard. Therefore, inasmuch as the last part of the motion simply desires a Teport on ways and means, and inasmuch as we know where the ways and means are to come from so far as the Dominion of Canada is to furnish them, namely out of the public treasury of this country, there seems to be no need for a resolution in this form. For this reason, I would have expected the Minister of Labour to say: I will propose to amend this motion by a more definite motion setting forth the absolute need of urgent and immediate action by the Dominion of Canada in order that Canada may no longer labour in this respect under t''e disadvantages from which she has suffered so long. Instead of that the Minister of Labour was constrained to suggest that the debate should be adjourned, that the motion should be, in effect, withdrawn, and that this session should pass without a single step being taken in this matter. I have thought it desirable to place this asnect of the question before the House. 1 say to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie 1 that I am entirely in sympathy with the object he ha., in view, that I trust action will be taken along the line he has suggested, if no other action can be taken, but so far as I am concerned I would greatly and infinitely prefer that a more definite and practical and speedy action should be taken than that which has been suggested in this resolution itself.

Mr. Speaker, I must say I was greatly surprised at the stand taken by the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) upon this question. I would have supposed that we would have taken this matter into consideration and would have placed an amount in the estimates to at least make a commencement on me line suggested bv the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). Therefore, I was .surprised that the minister should move to sidetrack this issue. The action of the minister shows that the government have decided to take no further interest in the subject this session, and I hope that the House will divide and let us see whether the Minister of Labour is to be supported in his effort to sidetrack this important issue.
Mr. MOBLEY CURRIE (Prince Edward
County). Mr. Speaker, the question Taised bv the resolution of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has been shown by the discussion this afternoon to be perhaps of as much importance to the industry and commerce of this country as that of the tariff. Resolutions and memorials have been mentioned which have been presented to this House to show the im-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
portance of the subject. I believe there a' e other indications which are perhaps of as great importance as these in showing the tendency of public opinion on this question. In the first place, I wish to reLc to the schools already established in the United States. We have there many schools for special industries, and a point which I believe is of importance is that there are in all parts of this country to-day young men who have learned their trades here and who are emigrating to the United States to take these courses in technical education in these schools. We have now stopped almost every other class of emigration to the United States, but with this one class we have not interfered, and I think it is high time that we took some steps to furnish our young men with the facilities which they are at present obliged to seek for in a foreign country. In the second Diace, it has been well said that the correspondence schools are attempting to carry out this work of technical education. That is very true, an immense amount of money is going to these schools. I do not believe that most people are aware of the number of men taking the courses in these correspondence schools. Some years ago I looked into this subject for a short time and I was surprised to find that one of these schools had enrolled as students at least 200,000 in the United States and Canada. That this large number of young men are attempting to obtain practical education in such an imperfect way shows the great need for education of this kind to-day.
I shad not discuss the importance of technical education; I believe wp are fully seized of that. What we have to discuss to-night is the question: Has the parliament of Canada a jurisdiction in this matter of technical education which it can take up and should take up and define? If it has such iurisdiction, I believe we should take advantage of the present occasion to take some steps in the direction of acting under that jurisdiction.
If the contention is raised, as I believe it was by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) that this parliament has jurisdiction in the actual work of instruction in technical education, I cannot agree with it for several reasons. From the- simple reading of the British North America Act it is seen that by article 91 the federal government is given jurisdiction over those subjects not assigned exclusively to the provinces, and by article 93 education is assigned exclusively to the provinces. Some say that education should be subdivided, that we have in technical education something different from ordinary education. But I believe that the result of the thought of the best men to-day on this subject is that there is actually no dividing line be-

tween cultural education and technical education, that the one merges insensibly into the other and that this attempt to differentiate technical and cultural education has been a great obstacle in the advancement of all systems of the former. Again, it has been said that we have examples already, such as the Royal Military College at Kingston. I draw attention to the fact that the latter part of article 91 of the British North America Act says that subjects coming within the classes of subjects assigned to the legislative authority of Canada shall not be deemed to come within the classes of subjects of a private character assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces, and it is only fair to consider the subject of military training as one which comes naturally within the jurisdiction of the Department of Militia and Defence. This being the case, in establishing the Royal Military College we have simply acted in accordance with the latter part of article 91 of the British North America Act. Again, in the case of agriculture, we see that by article 95 the Dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures are given concurrent jurisdiction, so that these two cases are exceptions and the rule, I think, judging by Die simple reading of the British North America Act, is that in the matter of actual instruction in technical education this parliament has no jurisdiction. However, I believe there is another and a more important reason why we should not interfere with the actual work of instruction in technical education. We have an example to go by in Germany. Thirty years ago they had the same discussion on the jurisdiction of the federal and state legislatures on technical education. At that time good reasons were given why technical education in Germany should be left to the states. In the first place, it grafted itself naturally on the system of common education; in the second place giving the states jurisdiction would give elasticity to the system, and in the third place, competition would be introduced. For these three reasons, the opinion of those who held that technical education should be placed under the jurisdiction of the states instead of the federal government in Germany had precedence. That action was taken in Germany on purely theoretical grounds. We have to-day the practical experience of Germany extending over a period of twenty or thirty years. The system has worked out splendidly and for that reason I believe we should not consider the advisability of this parliament undertaking any part of the actual instruction in the work of technical education. There is a third reason why I think we should not undertake that work and that is that we should be interfering with the excellent system of technical education which we already have
in embryo in the various provinces. The province of Nova Scotia and some of the other provinces have been referred to by preceding speakers and I wish for one moment to refer to the system in the province of Ortario. About a year ago there was a petition from the city of Brantford for the formation of industrial continuation classes in that city. This system of industrial continuation classes is a most important part of the system of technical education, and while I do not know what the result of the petition was, I know that it aroused discussion and every one feels today, in so far as industrial continuation classes go, that they are something that graft themselves naturally upon the public school system because these industrial continuation classes would utilize the public school buildings as well as many of the teachers and they would be simply for the most part classes continued in the public schools as they exist to-day. There is also a transformation going on in the province of Ontario in our high school system. We have a manual training department, a commercial department, an agricultural department, and it will probably be but a short time before we will have the remaining courses composed of the industrial, scientific and classical parts. When we have this one further change made in the high school system of Ontario, we will have the prototype of the gymnasia and the pro-gymnasia of the German system. In addition we have in Ontario the school of practical science in Toronto which corresponds with the third class of technical education in Germany represented by the great technical high schools. We have the fourth class represented in Germany by schools for particular industries and in Ontario this class is represented by the dairy school, the school of mines at Kingston and the agricultural college at Guelph. So, we have in Ontario already the skeleton of a system of technical education such as exists in the German states. For these reasons, for the reason that we have a good example in Germany of what can be accomplished by leaving the matter of technical instruction to the individual states, because of the reading of the British North America Act and from the fact that already we have in the provinces a system under way, I believe that this parliament will be very unwise in discussing seriously the question as to whether they have jurisdiction in this matter which would justify them in undertaking actual instruction in technical education. That being the case, the question arises:	Is there any function left
which this parliament can assume in the matter of technical education which would advance it? I want to refer to two or three things that I think are of some importance and which would result in some action be-

ing taken on the part of the parliament of Canada.
In the first place I want to say that if we took some action now we would define our exact position on this subject. It is evident to any one to-night that there is not a consensus of opinion as to what our exact position is, but if we took some action at the present time we would define that position and we would not have, as we had a year ago, the Minister of Education of the province of Ontario going about the country, making speeches, as reported in the press, to the effect that the province of Ontario were waiting to see what action the Dominion parliament would be prepared to take, before they took any action upon this matter of technical education. The mere fact that we have not already acted and defined our position has, for the time being, put off the discussion of the matter of technical education in Ontario, and I think that if this commission were appointed, or if some other action were taken by the government resulting in the definition of our position it would be an important thing for technical education in Ontario at least.
Eeference has been made in some of the speeches to the fact that this parliament would have it within its powers to grant money. While it is possible, I do not believe that it is an important subject. I just wish to refer in that connection for a moment to the cost of a system of technical education. The fact that we lay so much stress upon the granting of money for this purpose is owing to our belief that a system of technical education is a very expensive thing. Looking over a system such as that which exists in Germany we find that in some of the states the cost of the complicated system which they have there is between $200,000 and $300,000 a year. So that, I believe it fair to assume that a system of technical education could be established and put in a fair way of operation in any of the provinces for an annual expenditure of $100,000. That would not by any means be a very serious obstacle.
There is another reason and one which I think will appeal strongly to the Minister of Labour. In any consideration of the development of a system of technical education, as it exists in Germany, one is strongly impressed by the fact that unless you have the interest of the manufacturers and others interested in technical education aroused, the establishment of any system is bound to result in failure. You have to have the interest aroused first. You have to have a demand for a system before it can be a success. That being the case, I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I will be pardoned if I refer for a moment or two to some personal experiences. I have been interested in this subject for some time and

often in travelling over the country I take occasion to talk with manufacturers on the train and in other places in regard to this subject. I usually find that there is amongst manufacturers an idea that this subject is important, but they usually think that it is of importance to some other manufacture than their own. They have no personal interest in it from the standpoint of their own manufacture. I want to illustrate that bv a concrete example. In the part of the country that I have the honour to represent the manufacturing industry is represented chiefly by the canning factories where fruits and vegetables are canned. The first man to undertake that work was Mr. W. Boutter, in Prince Edward county, over twenty years ago, and since I was a boy I have had a chance of seeing these factories in actual operation. I have seen valleys converted into level ground by being filled with spoiled fruit that went bad in the process of manufacture. I have seen the site for a factory made out of a marsh by being filled with spoiled goods. If we had a system of technical education for the instruction of those interested in canning factories it would be a great advantage to that industry. With that object in view, about seven years ago, I wrote out as complete a plan as I could for the establishment of an institution of that kind in connection with the Agricultural college at Guelph, where, in their chemical and bacteriological laboratories, they have facilities for such a course. At the same time I explained to the Hon. John Dryden that it would, of course, be necessary to get the interest of the manufacturers in this subject. It may be that at that time we did not have such intelligent manufacturers as the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Marshall) and the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), but at any rate, after talking the matter over with them for six or seven years, I could never find any of them who would bring the subject to the attention of the Canners' convention. I only mention that to show that many _ of the manufacturers have not the active interest in the subject that they should have. It has been mentioned that steps have been taken in the United States to accomplish something in this matter of technical education. This brings me up to the point as to how it has been accomplished. The best work that has come into my hands on the auestion of technical education is the report of the commissioner of labour of the United States. That was distributed broadcast through the United States and has done more than any other one thing to give the people generally information on this subject and to stimulate the interest of all classes of people in it. There is a work that we can do, and I was very glad to hear that the Minister of Labour was about to collect material along this line. If the steps taken by the government re-
10S5

suited only in one thing and that was the Department of Labour being instructed to arouse the interest of manufacturers and others in this subject the establishment of that department would be a thing that we might be thankful for in the future. Therefore, I say that one of the great functions of this government is the stimulation of interest on the part of all classes in this great subject.
In the third place, there is something of a suggestion in a remark made by one of the speakers in regard to the Imperial Technical Institute of Berlin. This is a country of great resources; I think I am safe in saying that our undeveloped resoures are far and away greater than any we have yet developed. Our efforts should be directed towards developing our unknown resources and towards the utilization of the by-products of our different manufacturers which now go to waste. I believe it would be well within the jurisdiction of this parliament to establish a technical institute of the highest .class, and manned by men of the highest technical ability who would have as their duty the investigation of our unknown resources. For instance, just to mention only one out of the number, we have in Canada unlimited supplies of clay, felspar, and quartz which are the raw products of the china and porcelain industry, and I doubt if we have a single manufacturer of these articles in the Dominion. Again, if we look out of the windows of this building we ,can see at the mills on the other side of the river the great waste of sawdust which is going on, and it would be well within the duty of such an institute to devise means for its commercial utilization. I have been told that bearings could be made from this by-product which would be more useful than babbit metal or brass for the shafting of machinery. I will speak of only two examples of the utilization of by-products. Not many years ago a gentleman interested in the fish packing industry in Maine hired a young man named Lepage to look into some of the problems in connection with the curing fish, and within a year Mr. Lepage had discovered that a certain variety of glue could be made from the fish refuse, a simple discovery which resulted in his becoming a multi-millionaire. Take again the dye industry which has so enormously developed in Germany as a by-product of coal tar. As late as 1892, London had practically the monopoly of the indigo trade of the world, and Germany then imported about 4,000 tons of indigo yearly; but then came the discovery of Professor Hoffman, and to-day Germany produces three-fourths of the indigo product of the world, and instead of importing 4,000 tons a year, as formerly, she now exports 8,000 tons. The
experiments in connection with coal tar and other by-products have resulted in chemical discoveries which a year or two ago accounted for an export trade of about $200, 000,000 a year in Germany. In view of these results it is well that this parliament should consider the establishment of a Dominion institute of technology which would look to the development of our unknown resources and the utilization of the by-products of our existing manufactures.
Now, I believe that the general system of education in Canada is not excelled by that of any country in the world. The graduate in mathematics from one of our Canadian universities can go to one of the best schools in the United States and he will find that his Canadian mathematical training has resulted in putting him at least one year in advance of the graduate of Harvard, Yale or Princeton. If vou look at the curricula of the engineering schools of the United States you will find that mathematics are superficial and elementary compared with what is taught to the Canadian student. In the department of science you find the same condition. But when we want a man with high technical knowledge we have to take one of these American graduates who has been able to avail himself of the facilities afforded by technical education in the United States, although the ground work of his general education may be greatly inferior to that of the Canadian. It would be a grand thing for Canada if we were able to furnish our young men with the technical knowledge which would enable them to become great engineers and to erect, for example, such works as the Quebec bridge, without having to send for our experts to the United States. One Quebec bridge on top of the water instead of under the water would pay for a system of technical education in Canada for a long time.
Now, the function of the government of the German empire in connection with education is not, I fear, thoroughly understood in other countries. The pre-eminent function lies in the encouragement it gives to the associations of teachers and the associations of manufacturers and others interested in technical education, and under this system technical education in Germany has been unified and brought to its high standard. In most of the published works on technical education in Germany, in the English works at any rate, the assistance given by the German federal government to these associations is passed over as unimportant, while the Germans themselves look upon it from an entirely different view point. I notice that in the report of the Commissioner of Labour of the United States theTe are only a few lines dealing with this branch of the subject, and in consequence of this lack of information, until

three years ago the people of the United States were not seized of the importance of the relation of the federal government to the promotion of technical education. In the year 1906 there was formed the American association for the advancement of technical education in the United States, which at its second meeting in Chicago provided for an expenditure of $25,000 during the coming year for the advancement of technical education. At the second meeting of that association 18 states were represented, and at the third meeting every state in the Union had a representative present, so that our cousins across the line are now fully aware of the great importance of these federal associations for the advance of technical education. There again is a function which this parliament could assume. One of the recommendations of the American association at its second annual meeting was that the United States government should appoint a commissioner who would devote his entire time to a propaganda for the development and upbuilding of technical education throughout the states of the Union.
Now, Mr. Speaker, while I do not believe that the federal government has jurisdiction with regard to the actual instructional part of technical education, I do say that we can do something towards stimulating the interest of our Canadian people in this subject. I believe we could establish a chemical institution of the very highest order for the Dominion, and I believe we could give assistance to these large Dominion associations for the advancement of the cause. Perhaps in the future we might appoint a commission.	_ _
I was glad to hear from the Minister of Labour that the government was likely to give the matter serious consideration and I trust that the best men in the country will come to their aid. When this question became a very live one in Germany twenty years ago, Prince Bismarck did not consider it beneath him to give a great deal of his time and consideration to the question, and I shall quote a prediction made by Prince Bismarck at that time, After looking thoroughly into the subject, he said in substance that the nation which has technical schools has secured itself for commercial and industrial supremacy. That was said by Bismarck not twenty years ago, and at the present time we see that it has almost come true in Germany. I believe that will go down to history as one of the greatest predictions of one of the greatest statesmen. To-day we are giving a great deal of attention and thought to the matter of the Germany navy; but to-night we may well reflect that under the protecting influence of a system of technical education, Germany has already constructed a fleet of ironclads of commerce before which Mr. M. CURRIE.
the old wooden frigates of her commercial competitors have faded away like a toy flotilla. Mr. Speaker, I am in hearty sympathy with any effiorts which this parliament make make in forwarding a system of technical education in any way that lies within its jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and those of other hon. gentlemen in favour of technical education. Indeed the textile trade of Canada owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for South Wellington for introducing to this House this most important question. Speaking from practical experience, I can assure this House that it would be a great benefit to the textile trade of Canada if we had technical schools established in the various provinces where textile manufacturing is carried on. While I say that on behalf of the textile manufacturers, I fully agree that technical schools should be established for every other industry that is carried on in this great Dominion. One of the things the workmen of Canada lack is technical education, and there is very limited means of getting such an education in Canada at the present time.
The hon. member for South Wellington has referred to the fact that the coarse wools of Canada are exported to the United States. These wools are manipulated there in a manner in which they cannot be in Canada, because there are in the United States a better educated class of mechanics, men who have had a thorough technical training, to manipulate that kind of wool. I know of no class of manufacturers in Canada who suffer more for the want of technically educated men than the textile manufacturers. In England and Germany this class of people get a thorough technical education, and consequently they are able to manipulate cheap raw material in such a way as to make it into a good-looking article which is sent to this country to the detriment of the Canadian manufacturers. Nobody knows better than the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Customs the difficultes which Canadian manufacturers have to contend with along that line. Deputation after deputation have waited on these hon. gentlemen in the effort to get this state of affairs remedied. The hon. Minister of Finance told us this afternoon that we might expect the budget speech before the holidays. Well, I can assure him that the textile manufacturers, especially those engaged in the woollen industry, are looking forward to that speech with a great deal of interest, in the hope that some measure of relief may be given to them. However, the question we are dealing with to-night has nothing to do with

the tariff. This is a question on which we may be thankful to find both sides of the House heartily agreed. Consider the great beneficial results that have come from the agricultural colleges established in the different provinces of this Dominion. Young men attend those colleges and get a technical education, and then go back to their farms and produce more grain to the acre and a better quality of grain, and breed better classes of cattle and horses. There are young men from these colleges attending farmers institutes and giving lectures, thus educating the young men who attend these institutes, but who cannot afford to attend the agricultural colleges. If we get such beneficial results from agricultural colleges, military colleges, medical colleges and business colleges, why not have established in this country technical schools in order that the manufacturers of this country may receive from those colleges similar benefits to those received from colleges I have referred to. I do not wish to prolong this debate, because it is getting late, but I do want to take the opportunty, from a manufacturer's standpoint, of expressing my conviction that no institutions of learning could be established in Canada that would impart more useful knowledge than technical schools. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the government will see its way clear to appoint a commission asked for by the hon. member for South Wellington.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I had not the pleasure of being present in the earlier stages of the debate and consequently have missed a part of this very interesting discussion. I shall have to content myself with reading the earlier part of the debate in ' Hansard,' But what I have heard has enabled me to appreciate thoroughly the great importance of the subject under discussion. I must take exception entirely to the observation of an hon. gentleman opposite that the motion to adjourn is a motion to sidetrack this resolution; and while I propose to vote for the motion to adjourn, I do so on altogether a different ground. After the discussion we have had, after the abundance of information brought before the House, showing the great need of this movement in Canada, it would indeed be strange if nothing further should be done. We are all of the opinion that something should be done, and tire only question is what is the better way of doing it. I have no doubt that we have the power to spend our own money in the way we please. If, as a layman, I should venture to express an opinion on a constitutional question, I would on that point agree heartily with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition; but there may be room for doubt 35
as to whether we should organize the machinery for an elaborate educational system, even though we had the right to grant the money. It is not, however, necessary to enter on that branch of the question. If we agree that it is an important matter and something should be done, then it is for us to look about and see what is.the best way to do it. An hon. member of the opposition side said there should be no inquiry but that the Dominion should go right ahead and do something. Well, while appreciating the spirit that prompted the hon. gentleman to take that view, I do not agree in it at all. I think it is the duty of the provincial authorities in the first place to institute the work, but should they not do it efficiently, I do not say that the Dominion parliament should not step in and assist them. I am going to vote for the adjournment of the debate, not for the purpose of sidetracking the matter, but that we may have further opportunity of considering, not the wisdom of doing something, but the best way in which to do it. Take the province of Nova Scotia: that province has done a great deal of work and spent much money in the establishment of a system of technical education, and it would be eminently wise, before we proceed to deal with the question, to put ourselves in communication with its educational authorities and see how the Dominion and provincial authorities can work together. What is true of that province is equally true of the others. There is every desire on the part of the government to show our appreciation of this work, and I join most heartily in all I have heard this afternoon with regard to its necessity and importance, and in voting for the motion to adjourn, I do so in order that we may have the opportunity of considering further what is the best way to aid a movement which seems to have received the favour of the whole House.

Last year I asked the government some questions regarding its intention to establish some such institution in Ottawa or some other suitable part of Canada for the consideration of similar questions to those brought to our notice by the hon. member for South Wellington. There are three classes of technical education. One is such as might be granted by cities and municipalities for the development of artisans and mechanics along certain lines. The other would be such as come under the influence of the provincial authorities, for the development of matters purely connected with their own province; but there are many matters which evidently affect the Dominion as a commercial nation, a part of the great British empire, to be still closer connected with it in a very short time, I trust. These matters I think should be treated by the Dom-



inion at large. Let me name some of these, concerning which people from every part of the country are reaching for information. Take the question of the manufacture of steel. Patents are being held on the advanced processes of producing steel such as may drive every other industry, not using these advanced patents, out of the markets. Why should there not, - in connection with this development, be some institution at Ottawa where encouragement would be given and experiments carried on in order that the highest perfection might be attained in this very important industry? Only last year two patents were brought out, each of which, in its own sphere, practically revolutionized the trade and put every industry not using it at the mercy of those who do. The same may be said regarding copper. Then there is the question of sewage disposal. It is estimated by competent authorities that in a very few years our farms will he depleted of fertilizing elements and there will be nothing at the disposal of our farmers with which to replace them. I understand that the Americans are making gigantic strides in this regard. They are producing bacteria which, when mixed with the grain when sown, will draw the nitrogen from the atmosphere, and thus encourage the plant's life. There are various other processes of uniting carbon and phosphate with nitrogen. Why should not this government take up this matter, which is of vital interest to this country as a farming community, and have the experiments carried on in a government institution. I might also point to the question of producer gas being made from peat and all the various industries in that connection, which have been referred to by the Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman). All our great northern country is rich in peat. Why should not the government pay the cost of carrying on these experiments in their establishments in the city of Ottawa, and thus save the cost to the individual. If this peat could be utilized profitably, it would place Canada in the front rank of manufacturing communities by giving us power cheaper even than the electricity from water-power. Moreover our supply of coal in central Canada depends on the United States. If peat could be profitably utilized for fuel, we would be absolutely independent of the United States in that regard. The experiment of utilizing peat should be conducted by the government. I know three or four gentlemen who have carried on experiments to develop that industry, and they lost their money. It ought to be the duty of the government to carry out these things in the experimental stages.
Every one knows that the dyeing and the dyes used in the trades and manufactures are also of very great importance to the development of the nation. There should be a scientific branch in connection with Mr. HUGHES.
the government to take up all this class of work. Progress in mining knowledge is being made all over the world, but I believe that if the government established an institution with highly skilled officers, advancement would be made very much more efficiently than by mere hap-hazard work on the part of individuals in mines here and there over the country. A very interesting matter was brought to my notice yesterday by Mr. Murray of Toronto. He had given an address in Montreal a few days before on the chemistry of the wool trade, a subject of which I had never heard before, but an explanation showed me that in this line there was a very important interest for the whole Dominion of Canada and an absolute need of a scientific investigation into the whole business. Then there is the development of nickel. One could mention a score of other branches of commercial industry all of which could be improved by having a bureau or a school of technology, an institute of some kind in Ottawa or elsewhere, where the best men in the country could be kept, even at high salaries. I am certain the country would endorse such an expenditure and it would be justified by the results.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) expressed a strong desire to do something. He said the Dominion government recognized the importance of the subject and had all the information necessary to deal with it. It seems strange to me if the government are so anxious to do something, the Minister of Labour, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) are also anxious to do something, they should forget that we had a long discussion on this two years ago. At that time most of the members were anxious to see something done, but it was shelved in much the same way as it is being shelved to-night and we heard nothing more of it until to-night. The motion was placed on the Order Paper last year on January 28, it remained there until May 19, when we prorogued, but nothing was done. Now we have had the motion discussed at great length for the third time, and the_ Minister of Labour admits it is so very important he drew arguments from China and Japan and told us of the danger we were confronted with to-day from the industrial life of China. What was the remedy? To Christianize the Chinese so they would work less and keep more Sabbaths and I presume let the Canadians fall into the Chinese habits, work longer hours, and keep fewer Sabbaths, and then we would be able to compete with them. If it is so important that we should do so much to help the labouring class in this country why is it that the minister who is at the head of a department brought into being for that especial purpose, has allowed the whole summer to go

by and has permitted one of the most unfortunate disputes between capital and labour that this country has experienced to continue, apparently without making any effort to bring it to a close. I thought that he might have been of value to the country in this matter but he did not seem desirous to make any effort to be valuable. He will elaborate great theories and present strong arguments to the House on lines on which he is making no effort whatever to help the people. I think that if he had more of the practical in him and less of the theory it would be to better purpose. This is the third year we are going to sidetrack this question. How long will it be before it will be taken up in a practical way by the present government. The ministers admit that they have all the information that is required, but beyond collecting that information there is no effort on tile part of the government to doing anything.

I have pleasure in adding my voice to those raised in favour of the resolution of the hop. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that this matter of the appointment of a commission on technical education be decided forthwith as opposed to the suggestion in amendment of the Minister of Labour that the matter should be indefinitely postponed. The Minister of Labour at least has the excuse that he was not personally cognizant of, and was not a party personally to the promises made by this government to the representatives of organized labour in Canada when early in this year they interviewed Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Lemieux, as representing the government and laid before them a series of requests for legislation which the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada desired to have passed. Replying to that delegation on the subject of technical education, Mr. Lemieux, on the 12th of January, 1909, nearly a year ago, stated, according to the published official report of the Trades and Labour Congress, that the appointment of a commission on technical education was under consideration. To my mind it is surprising that other members of the government who must be cognizant of the promise made by the Prime Minister and the then Minister of Labour, have not corrected the present Minister of Labour in the extraordinary position he takes on this occasion, and that when for the third year in succession the promoters of the idea of a commission on technical education come to this parliament they are told that they must wait indefinitely until the government gives consideration to this matter. As one of those interested in promoting the cause of technical education, interested particularly in seeing that effect is parliament to the desires of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada 35}
I must say that I can only regard the suggestion made to-night to adjourn the debate as evidence of the intention of the government to resist the suggestion to participate in the movement for technical education and to shelve the matter indefinitely. If there is any intention on the part of the government to appoint a commission later in the session I think it would well become some minister to tell us of that fact, to take us into his confidence and give us some reason for supporting the suggestion that instead of pressing the motion on the Order Paper we shall wait until it suits the pleasure of the government to tell us when the appointment is to be made. While I rose mainly to call attention to the definite statement made on the 12th of January last that the government had then under consideration the appointment of just such a commission. I wish to refer to one or two incidents brought out in the same report of the Trades and Labour Congress. The present Minister of Labour honoured that congress with his presence and he obtained, as might be expected, because the report of his eloquence had reached the congress before him, a most hearty reception. We read that the Minister of Labour received a tremendous ovation on entering the chamber. He made reference to many of the points the congress had under discussion and he also referred particularly to a matter which he has brought before us to-night." We heard with great interest that there was no other way under Heaven by which we could be saved from the menace of oriental competition except the adoption of some active measures in connection with technical education. We find that when the Minister of Labour addressed the congress he had a different idea as to what we should do to save ourselves from Chinese competition. We find it expressed in this extraordinary way:
He also referred to investigations conducted by the home and Canadian governments in China, and gave a brief synopsis of his observations while assisting in conducting these investigations in China, and stated that it might be well for the representatives of labour to study the effect the poll tax of $500 Canada had placed upon the Chinese was having upon the trade which the manufacturers of Canada were endeavouring to develop in China and the Orient.
Now when we contrast that as a chief menace to our trade with the orient in September last, with the statement to-night that the one thing we must do to save ourselves from oriental competition is to adopt a scheme of technical education, I think _we must come to the conclusion that the Minister of Labour, at least, is not serious. We find that the Trades and Labour Congress have a very different idea as to what this government means when it postpones from time to time the action which

their representatives have urged upon this House. We have a report in this book on the Bill introduced by the congress respecting an eight-hour law on government contracts; and on that occasion, as we}l as on this, the bug-a-boo of provincial rights was introduced as a reason why we should not deal with it. We find the parliamentary committee thus reporting:
His argument (speaking of the Hon. Mr. Lemieux) as to interference with provincial rights was answered by himself when he said that we could only pass such legislation as regards public works. That is all Mr. Ver-ville's Bill dealt with. But in any event there would be no conflict with provincial jurisdiction. The government did not think of provincial rights when it enacted the fair-wage clause nor when it made provision to prevent sweat-shop labour being employed on government work. There is no more conflict in the one case than in the other, and as for ' respect for the usages and customs ' of different localities, the very reason given, during the discussion of the fair-wage clause, by the then Minister of Labour, was, that the government should be a model employer and an example to other employers. It is all very well to refer to the dignity of labour, but it would be a greater compliment to assume that labour is intelligent enough to see through such arguments as those used by the Hon. Minister of Labour in the discussion of this Bill. The debate served a useful purpose at all events in showing what we have to meet when the Bill is next introduced.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to members of this House to remove from it the reproach levelled at it by the Trades and Labour Congress when they say in this official report that when the labour representatives introduced this Bill it was trifled with, and subterfuges instead of solid facts were advanced why it should not be dealt with. I say let us be men. If we are in favour of a grant for technical education, let us say so, to-night. If we are not in favour of it, let us be manly enough to say that we will not take up this matter, that the provinces must bear the sole burden, and that we will pay no heed to the resolution of the Trades and Labour Congress. Let us say so openly, and not put them off with the suggestion that this matter shall be postponed till some indefinite time. In conclusion I will read the request which is now before the government from the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada with respect to technical education.
Resolved, that this congress emphatically reaffirm its declaration in favour of the immediate appointment by the Dominion government of a commission on technical education, and that copies of this resolution be immediately sent to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Minister of Labour.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
I wish to say a few words in regard to that question. Though I sympathize with the idea which has inspired the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), I confess that I cannot agree with the motion as it is framed. Therefore, if the wording of that motion were put to the vote on its own merit, I would be obliged to vote against it, whereas I am in favour of the proposed adjournment. We know bat everything relating to education is under the jurisdiction of the local governments, and for my part I would like the authority to remain vested with those governments. I do not want the federal government to interfere later on with our education affairs.
Just now we are secure from all danger with regard to education. I am anxious to keep for my province its self-government in its integrity, and I believe that all the other provinces are anxious also to preserve their autonomy. I would not therefore let anybody infringe upon it.
We have heard so much talk about the question of separate schools that we should not desire that matter to be brought up again. Our system is perfectly good, and 1 confess that I am against that motion if it is intended to deprive us of our rights with regard to education. If, on the contrary, the question is for the federal government to interfere only m order to give moneys with a view to assist provinces in the establishment of technical schools, I shall approve the motion, provided the moneys be given to the provincial governments and they have the right to control the appropriation of the funds and to manage them as they think proper, but not otherwise.
I think this motion is actually dangerous, because if it were adopted we in favour of separate schools would find ourselves, later on, in a very bad position.
As I have already said, if I were obliged to vote on the merits of this proposition, I would vote against it. But as the question is on the adjournment of the debate, I am in favour of this latter motion.

As mover of the resolution I may say a word on the motion to adjourn. After dealing with the question somewhat fully this afternoon, and endeavouring to impress upon the government the propriety of the motion, and also the expediency of appointing a commission forthwith, I hardly think it would be consistent for me now to vote for the postponement of my own motion. However, I accept in absolute good faith the statement made by the Minister of Labour in asking for an adjournment of this debate in order to give the government further time to consider the question. If I thought there was the slightest foundation for the statement of the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. DECEMBER 6, 1909
Reid) I would be the more inclined to press the matter with all the resources at my command. But I accept the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, and the positive assurance given to this House by the Minister of Finance that the government does feel in sympathy with the main purpose of this resolution, but requires further time for consideration. I was somewhat amused by the statement of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who seemed to complain that on this occasion there was a possibility of adjourning the debate, and that the question had been similarly adjourned indefinitely on a former occasion; and if the few members who were present on the former occasion were here now, they will perhaps also be surprised when they are told that the hon. member who moved the adjournment of the debate and postponed the question on that occasion, was my hon. friend from East Grey.
I might just state that while I myself am reasonably clear as to the constitutional rights of this parliament to go as far as this motion asks-and I am glad to know that I am supported in this view by the hon. leader of the opposition-I can tell the leader of the opposition that the gentleman who sits immediately to his right is not so clear. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) was good enough, at the six o'clock adjournment, to compliment me on the general tenor of my remarks but he saw fit to say that on the constitutional question I talked utter nonsense. So that, there is some difference of opinion on that subject also. However, as I feel satisfied that the government has evidently the intention of going ahead on this matter and desires only time for consideration, I do not ask any one to support what may be my vote if a division is taken. I would, for the sake of consistency, if there is a decision, have to vote for my motion, but I do not do so with the idea of antagonizing the government or of placing myself in a false position with regard to it. I realize that antagonizing the government cannot help the matter at all. I desire the support of the government, I desire the government to act, as I desire my motion to be carried out, whether amended or not, after consideration.
House divided on the amendment of Mr. King.
